LOCAL（国内）
NEWS
ALM（コジマ録音）から新作２タイトル・リリース
八巻志帆『EVOKE』とマックス・デヴロー『レジスタンス』
2026年7月5日
編集部

ALM（コジマ録音）からユニークな新作２タイトルがリリースされる。バスクラリネット奏者八巻志帆の『EVOKE』とエレクトリック・ギター奏者マックス・デヴローの『レジスタンス』。

心のなかの音に、もういちど出会う

『EVOKE』（ALM3138) は八巻志帆の４作目のアルバム、八巻と中村奈央の２バスクラリネットによるフロントが、柳原由佳 (p) 、伊東佑希 (b)、則武諒 (ds) のピアノ・トリオと組むクインテット。18年にわたってバスクラリネットと向き合ってきた八巻が自身の音楽観をあらためて見つめ直した先に生まれたアルバムで、ジャズやクラシックなどのボーダーを超えてバスクラリネットを媒介として紡がれる音楽の美しさを、オリジナルやカヴァーを通して、きわめて率直な形で提示する。

試聴サイト；
https://kojimarokuon.com/products/alm-3138?_pos=2&_sid=3313df8c3&_ss=r

「抵抗」を原理としたプロセスと音楽

ミネアポリスを拠点とする作曲家・ギタリスト、マックス・デヴロー（1994–）は、映像・絵画・いけばなまで手がける分野横断的アーティストで、現代アメリカのアヴァンギャルド・シーンで独特の存在感を放つ。現代音楽、電子音響、サウンド・スタディーズ（音響文化論）の交点に位置するリリースは日本を含む各国レーベルから100を超え、坂本弘道、羽野昌二、吉田隆一といった日本の即興・前衛音楽アーティストとの協働も重ねている。本作《レジスタンス》は2026年作曲、デヴロー自演のギター独奏によってリアライゼーションされた音源。音楽のストーリー性ではなく発音方法・持続的注意・時間の物質性を強調する思弁的かつ透徹とした音響作品。不特定楽器またはアンサンブルのための図形記譜は、作品の個の強度と同一性を保ちながら、同時に分断を越えた連帯とヴァリエーションの可能性に開かれている。（本作の図形楽譜をブックレットに収載）

items.body: Last year we were introduced to the Ibiza-based NGO MusicForTheSea through Coco Francavilla’s liquid re-oceaning. This year the imprint’s second release was also unveiled on United Nations World Oceans Day, and celebrates the ocean while drawing essential attention to conservation efforts. Tidal Shifts – Reimagine, an outgrowth of an event in Nice, is a collaborative effort among field recordists, composers, and visual artists, incorporating copious underwater recordings from the Strait of Gibraltar captured by the Institute of Marine Research of the University of Cádiz. These recordings lie at the heart of the release, calling one’s ears ever back to the sounds of the sea. IDRA eases us gently into the ocean, beginning at the shore; the waves lap beside twinkling electronics and placid keys. Considering how many ambient tracks from Ibiza have showcased the sound of waves, it’s amazing that so few are this intentional; instead of mere background or sound effect, they are the music’s reason to exist. The soundings of Oora introduce the human element, studying the health of the ecosystem; the waves are louder, as is the rolling of the hull. This is the sound of research rather than intrusion, evidence of scientists hard at work. The “Tides at Bay of Fundy” are the world’s highest, yielding real-time evidence of glacial melt and climate change. As the music grows more active, one can imagine the tide rising, quicker and higher than expected, a parable for the planet’s possible fate. At the very end, there is only the sound of water, along with the sounding instrument; the music has abruptly recessed. Whalesong launchhes Vito Gatto‘s “Introimmersion,” wrapping the listener in a watery blanket. Cascades of keys pass by like schools of fish. Brass enters in the second minute, along with the crackle of what may be brine shrimp. The implication is of something dark and enormous; the question is, benign or threatening? Is this simply the shadow of a passing whale, or the longer shadow cast by the Great Pacific Garbage Patch? The closing “Indigo Reverie” is a collaboration between Kazuya Nagaya and Coco Francavilla, the former fresh from the release of Lumina. During this contemplative piece, one may indeed become lost in one’s thoughts, dreaming of the ocean and weekends by the sea. But to only do so is to miss the point. 15% of the world’s population lives by a coastline, while three times that number visit every summer. The coastline – as well as the health of the sea – is endangered, as are the lives of those who live in and around it. Tidal Shifts may sound comforting, but its intent is to unsettle, or at the very least to motivate. The beauty of “Indigo Reverie” is that it grows like a coral reef; but the music seems always fragile, a reminder that without care, even the most durable facets of life can disintegrate. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by kev rowland — 'Fractal Guitar 4' is the fourth instalment in the 'Fractal Guitar' series which Swiss composer and guitarist Stephan Thelen initiated in 2015, with the last chapter being released in 2022. This is not the only series he has been working on and along with separate projects this is his 13th release since the first, which in itself was his 12th solo album outside of his work with Sonar. On this he again has multiple guests, many of whom he has worked with before, with only Norwegian guitarist Eivind Aarset playing on every track alongside Thelen, with the others contributing here and there. These include American guitarist Jon Durant, Israeli drummer Yogev Gabay, Markus Reuter from Germany (touch guitar), Fabio Anile from Italy (electric piano), Stefan Huth from Germany (touch bass guitar), Giri Subramaniam from India (tabla) and Andi Pupato from Switzerland (percussion), so a truly international line-up.When I started listening to this the first person I thought of was Allan Holdsworth, and that stayed true through the whole album although at times I also thought of John McLaughlin. One thing I found fascinating in that of all those involved, including Thelen himself, the musician I listen to most is Markus Reuter in multiple projects, yet here he is playing a role as opposed to driving music in his own manner, so his distinctive style is somewhat subsumed into the whole. One of the things which is fascinating with this album are the time signatures and polyrhythms being used, where musicians can actually be placing different signatures against each other which should lead to chaos both in the studio and in the brain but somehow it works, and I have no logical explanation as to why.If Gabriel was a guitarist as opposed to a singer I could imagine some of his early 80's albums sounding something like this, while King Crimson fans will also discover plenty here to enjoy as this is hugely complex and complicated, a music theorist's wet dream, yet there is also a clarity which makes it enjoyable as opposed to a chore. I cannot say this is overly easy to listen to, and is not for everyone, but if you want to hike through the pass less travelled you will find much more beauty than those who stay on the highways.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — This compilation is designed to provide an overview of Space Debris, a still active Krautrock band from Germany. Three of the nine tracks on the triple vinyl set from FdeM, which is already sold out by the way, are more than 20 minutes long while the set is more than two hours in length. If you can find a copy it also comes with a 24 pp A4 booklet, although you may find it easier to search out the digital version which also has two additional numbers. Formed in 2002 by two friends, Tommy Gorny (guitar) and Christian J�ger (drums), to play improvised music inspired by the Seventies' Krautrock and Psychedelic bands, they were joined by keyboard player Winnie Rimbach-Sator in 2008 and have had a few bassists, although Vroni Frisch has been there for the last decade. However, this material predates her arrival, stretching all the way back to 2005, with "Villamountain" hailing from 2012 and is the only previously unreleased material.I had not heard of this band prior to receiving the album, but I don't feel too bad given that label boss and Krautrock connoisseur Keith Jones only came across them about a year ago. The compilation was put together by the band themselves and shows that while they may be more underground than most, that is not down to lack of ability. Given this is generally improvised it is interesting to hear just how direct and together this album is and feels far more structured than many of the live composition works I come across. Gorny is often the lead melody, the keyboards are there to provide counterpoint and something to work against, the bass is the warmth glue which keeps it all together and then there are drums which are much more like a lead instrument in their own right as opposed to "just" holding it all together.They have been likened to the spirit of early Deep Purple (think "Mandrake Root"), Hendrix, Pink Floyd and Can while others have pointed towards 'Bitches Brew', and there is certainly a heavier relationships with bands like these as opposed to �resund Space Collective which is more dramatically Space Rock in nature. This is a fascinating album which deserves to be listened to on headphones when one has the time to really get inside what is going on, and fans of Krautrock certainly need to discover these guys if they have yet to come across them.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Vocalist Marco Cecioni brought experience from his earlier stint with the 1960s band Battitori Selvaggi to the formation of Il Balletto di Bronzo; their album Sirio 2222 is a compendium of influences carried over from that decade, such as psychedelia and the sound of Jimi Hendrix, delivered by a razor-sharp quartet that sounded both tight and energetic.The album kicks off with the rock-oriented "Un Posto" and the bluesy "Eh Eh Ah Ah"; while "Neve Calda" may not offer many compositional complexities, it captures that epic 1960s style, alongside drummer Giancarlo Stinga's Mitch Mitchell-esque playing. Influences of Eric Burdon & The Animals can also be traced."Ma Ti Aspetter�" borders on hard rock, reminiscent of early Black Sabbath, though the bass playing displays a distinctly jazzy fluidity."Meditazione" is something different; it features string arrangements by Giacomo Simonelli, and Marco Cecioni delivers a spot-on vocal performance, even if the composition itself isn't particularly remarkable. However, the track truly takes flight when the clavichord enters, raising the bar in a way that foreshadows the definitive album that would follow this one.Girotondo's psychedelic jams infused with pop melodies flowed naturally and made for enjoyable listening, yet the quartet could also turn wild, as seen in "Incantesimo," where those same improvisations took on a heavy blues feel, much like in "Ti Risveglierai Con Me." (It was used as the soundtrack for the Italian crime film Five Dolls for an August Moon, a prime example of giallo cinema directed by Mario Bava, that same year.)"Missione Sirio 2222" is the album's most ambitious composition, alongside "Meditazione", steeped in a floating psychedelia that refuses to settle on anything solid; the guitar and vocals sustain it until the track returns to a psychedelic rock sound.While it can be enjoyed for what it is, 1960s psychedelic rock, it gives no indication of the peak reached by their subsequent work, which would earn them a place in the Italian progressive rock scene before Marc, their singer and guitarist, left for Stockholm to pursue a career as a painter and graphic artist.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A growth in compositional maturity is evident on the second album by Mimmo Di Martino (guitar), Ettore Vigo (piano and organ), Martin Grice (saxophone and flute), Marcello Reale (bass), and Peppino Di Santo (drums and percussion). Jazz influences persist, albeit with a certain darkness, and the addition of the saxophonist truly adds greater compositional weight. While "Tremori Antichi" is a pleasant ballad, especially when sung in Italian, "Gioia, Disordine, Risentimento" demonstrated a more restless compositional spirit, once again driven by the saxophone.The album then alternates with simpler songs, such as "La Mia Pazzia," which captures that bohemian, communal vibe so popular at the time."Sogno" is another lovely ballad featuring backing vocals, though it moves away from the uptempo acoustic jazz style that suited them so well and where their true strength lay; this becomes apparent when they shine once more during the jazz improvisation in the second half of the track."Dimensione Uomo" is driven by piano and double bass, accompanied by acoustic guitar and backing keyboards, and sung with great feeling by Mimmo Di Martino."Culto Disarmonico" gives free rein to the band's jazz aspirations, with percussion and saxophone once again playing starring roles.Although the album lacks the clear focus of its predecessor, which leaned heavily into the acoustic sound, or its successor, which revisited that style with a more progressive edge, Lo Scemo e Il Villaggio, remains an enjoyable listen, offering that warm, epic, and quintessentially Italian flavor; the album's true gem comes at the end with "Pensiero Per Un Abbandono," featuring the Mellotron, a Renaissance-style piano, and a performance by Mimmo Di Martino that is present in both body and spirit.

items.body: U.K. alternative noise quartet Death Cult Electric have released their debut double album “Cult Classic”, a 15-track set issued on 26 June 2026 across two volumes through Black Maraca Records, with distribution by Symphonic Distribution. The band, fronted by producer Steffan Pringle, mix hyper-distorted post-punk, alternative rock and industrial-edged noise. Cult Classic (Vol I) by Death Cult Electric Cult Classic (Vol II) by Death Cult Electric Death Cult Electric split ‘Cult Classic’ across two volumes “Cult Classic” runs 15 tracks over two volumes. The first volume holds eight, opening with “Deleter” and moving through “Wishy Washy”, “The FinePrint”, “Lucifer in the Sky with Diamonds”, “In Infrared”, “Ooops! Wrong Planet”, “We are not Bees” and “She Comes too Quick”. The second volume, “Cult Classic (Vol II)”, adds seven: “Alligators”, “Moolah”, “Snakes and their Children”, “I’m So Cool……”, “Let’s Nightmare!”, “A.I Duplicate” and “Burn Bubblegum”. The set pulls together singles the band issued over several years, among them “Deleter”, “The FinePrint”, “She Comes too Quick” and “A.I Duplicate”, alongside newer tracks. Steffan Pringle recorded and mixed the album, mastered to a loudness of 6.66 LUFS. Press material for the release describes it as “It’s like if Nick Cave, Mark E Smith, Andy Falkous, and Guy McKnight became one channeling Big Black and holding Queens of the Stone Age by the throat. […] it rages so hard.” Both volumes are available digitally on Bandcamp and through the band’s Spotify page. About Death Cult Electric Death Cult Electric are a U.K. alternative noise quartet from Cardiff, built around Steffan Pringle, a producer and former member of the Welsh group Estrons who has also produced Adwaith and Himalayas. The current line-up features Pringle alongside Richard Wright, Alec Rees and Christopher Hampson. The group cite Sonic Youth and The Jesus Lizard among their reference points and have shared stages with Pulled Apart By Horses, Mclusky and Midasuno. items.body: Dirk Da Davo will forever be associated with The Neon Judgement, the legendary Belgian band that remains a benchmark and a source of inspiration for countless artists and fans. It was therefore quite a challenge when Dirk released the debut album of his new project, Neon Electronics, In 1999. While it never quite achieved the same level of recognition as The Neon Judgement, it is fair to say that, particularly in its early years, the project sounded both innovative and visionary. Twenty-six years later, the EP/mini-album “Liberation” was released and immediately announced as Neon Electronics’ final new production. The band—which for many years featured Glenn Keteleer and Pieter-Jan Theunis alongside Dirk Da Davo—had decided to call it a day. Over the course of a quarter-century, Neon Electronics built up an impressive body of work. Their original Techno-EBM sound gradually evolved, and “Liberation” ultimately brings the story full circle, returning to where it all began for Dirk: 80s influences transformed into strong, memorable songs infused with a powerful sense of nostalgia. Released by the Spanish label Oráculo Records, the record strikes me as a compelling sonic epitaph. I spoke with Dirk Da Davo about this final chapter, but our conversation explored much more besides. (Picture credits by Patrice Hoerner / Interview courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Liberation by NEON ELECTRONICS Dirk Da Davo / Neon Electronics interview Q: Hi Dirk, I’d actually like to start with what might otherwise have been the last question of this interview: what now? What else would you still like to achieve musically? Dirk: That’s an interesting question to start with! I look back and feel satisfied with a musical career of 45 years. I am happy to have had the top of my career in a time when the Electro-Punk and Rock & Roll level was still significantly higher in the music scene. I have travelled around the world, played in amazing locations and had the opportunity to collaborate with some very talented musicians. For example, the collaboration with my childhood hero Jean-Marie Aerts under DDDJMX is something I’m very proud of. Also a lot of fun, more recently, was the remix I made for Luc Van Acker, as well as my solo releases. What I never did before, and so still to be achieved, is composing music for a movie. I still would like to do that. So yes, they can call me 🙂 Q: The announcement of the end of Neon Electronics came as a surprise to me. Had you seen this coming for a while, and what ultimately influenced your decision? Dirk: I started collaborating with Glenn Keteleer (aka Radical G) 15 years ago. A few years later Pieter-Jan Theunis joined us on bass guitar. I enjoyed working and playing with these guys a lot. The decision to stop the project has grown over the last year. We decided to make one final album, but it had to be a good one. And so, we started working on the final Neon Electronics EP “Liberation” which got released recently. The album is the perfect harmony between 3 talented musicians, with each their own unique style and therefore in my opinion a very interesting and very good album. Q: I think it’s fair to say that you have always had a critical perspective on the evolution of music. Just consider the decline of the physical format, the rise of digitalization and streaming platforms, the abundance of software to make music, and now the growing presence of AI and social media. How do you view these developments with all your experience, to what extent did they influence your decision to stop Neon Electronics, and might they also affect the continuation of your musical career? Dirk: It is true that I am not known for my optimism 🙂 And a critical perspective has simply been part of my education, influenced and stimulated by my late father. I will never lose my critical view on music, nor on society in general. It is the essence of my personality, and it has always affected my musical style. For sure, these changes, how the music scene has evolved, by some defined as progress, by others as destruction, have played a part in the decision to close the Neon Electronics chapter. Do not understand me wrongly, I will keep on making music, music is my therapy. But let’s say that I am happy not to be an 18-year-old musician at the start of his career who needs to compete with soulless AI music, and whose success is measured in the quantity of likes on social media. Q: When you started out as a young musician in the early 1980s, Electronic music and its accompanying underground scene were a genuine phenomenon—something many people who experienced it still look back on with nostalgia, and perhaps even longing. How do you look back on that era? And is there still such a thing as a true underground scene today, or is everything now measured by streaming numbers, sales figures, algorithms, and increasingly standardized expectations? Dirk: The eighties were so interesting from a creative point of view. You had all these cult labels like 4AD, Factory Records, Les Disques Du Crépuscule, and many more, releasing vinyl after vinyl with interesting and often obscure music. There was an opportunity to be experimental, to think out of the box, and that’s how some of the best music of all times has been born. For the artists at the time, these labels created perspective; these times it was still possible to launch a career from the very deep underground scene. An underground scene or a countermovement will always exist. Nothing makes me happier than discovering music from young Punky musicians. Last week I received a message from a 15-year-old very cool girlie bass player. She said The Neon Judgment still is an inspiration for her play. This fills me with hope. Q: The first Neon Electronics release dates back to 1999. How do you look back on a journey that lasted more than a quarter of a century, and what are the highs and lows that immediately come to mind? Dirk: The year 1999 was a turning point in my musical career. It was year I started my own label DancedelicD, with the help of some cyber-IT punks. It also was the year that Neon Electronics was born. Did you know that the first Neon Electronics concert (@ Rumba, Leuven, Belgium – 1999) has been streamed Live on the Internet? This was quite revolting at the time, and the path towards independency had been set. The Neon Electronics journey has been interesting, it gave me the freedom to explore new boundaries, to try some different styles, to collaborate with different artists, … Q: How difficult—or perhaps how easy—was it to launch a new project after spending so many years with the legendary The Neon Judgement, especially considering that the new project’s name still contained a reference to it? Dirk: This has not always been easy, especially in the beginning. I wanted to re-build my own musical identity, and in a certain way liberate myself from the ubiquitous expectations connected to the name The Neon Judgement. Choosing the difficult way has always been my style: -) But at the same time, I wanted to stay loyal to my fans, and therefore the Neon referral stayed in Neon Electronics. Like Neon with a twist, you don’t always know what to expect. Q: Neon Electronics went through several different phases in terms of influences and line-up, which also resulted in albums that could sound quite distinct from one another. What did this project represent for you in terms of artistic expression, musical influences, and personal evolution? Dirk: Indeed, over the last 25 years Neon Electronics has known different line-ups. As an artist I feel the need to step out of the safety zone and to try something new. Back in the days I was experimenting with a new way of bringing live music, like a semi-DJ-set with live instruments and vocals. During the 90s I went clubbing a lot, which had its influence on Neon Electronics, back then you could feel its connection with Techno and sometimes even with House music or, Dance music in general. A few years later I felt again like playing in a band, and that resulted in the actual line-up with Glenn and PJ. Neon Electronics – Press photo 2019 Q: When you started Neon Electronics, I had the distinct feeling that you were doing something innovative, something that could also be heard at the time in the work of artists such as The Hacker, Terence Fixmer, David Carretta, The Horroris ao. Looking back, how innovative do you think it really was? Dirk: Thank you for the compliment. Indeed, freedom and innovation were definitely the driving forces at the start of Neon Electronics. Being different and being independent. This Electro-Punk attitude can be heard very clearly in the first Neon Electronics album. Q: Earlier this year, you released the EP/mini album “Liberation”, which I consider one of your strongest works in years. It combines influences that reach back to the roots of the 80s while presenting them within a contemporary sound. What did you still want to express with this release, and did you already know at the time that these would be the final songs of the project? Dirk: We are also very happy about the way “Liberation” turned out. It reflects how we are and how we want to be as artists. We respect our 80s background but chose for a contemporary sound. Yes, we knew that it would be our final release while creating the songs. The album was meant to be a crossover between Dark-Wave and modern beats, I think we succeeded quite well. Glenn did a great production job, and PJ’s contributions are always amazing. The remixed work from Patrick Codeyns (Front 242) and the Techno remix from Ancient Methods are a nice extra. Q: If you had to choose one Neon Electronics song at this very moment that best represents the project for you, which one would it be, and why? Dirk: It is too difficult to choose only one! They are all my babies. Because the different styles and different line-ups reflect me as an artist, I would choose one from the very beginning and one of our recent works: “Total Wam Bam” (“Neon Electronics”, 1999) & “Justification Unknown” (“Liberation”, 2026). About Neon Electronics Neon Electronics is a Belgian electro-wave and EBM project led by Dirk Da Davo, born Dirk Timmermans, co-founder of The Neon Judgement. The project started in 1999 as a solo project after Da Davo’s work with The Neon Judgement, the Leuven band he formed in 1981 with Frank Vloeberghs, also known as TB Frank. Neon Electronics was created as a separate outlet for electronic dance music. DancedelicD, the label founded by Dirk, describes the project as “electronic dance music without being specific house or techno”. The project’s sound moved between electro-wave, EBM, technoid electronics, post-punk references and guitar-based material. In a 2019 Side-Line interview, Da Davo said: “With Neon Electronics everything is possible, no limits, all freedom!” The first Neon Electronics release was the self-titled album “Neon Electronics” in 1999. “System Rivièra” followed in 2003, with “Swingers Delight” released in 2004 as a live recorded DJ mix CD. The project continued with “Monkey Ever After” in 2006 and “Ever After Monkey” in 2007. “Better Way EP”, a collaboration with The Hacker, was issued in 2009, while “Keylogger” followed in 2012. “Toyboy EP” appeared in 2013, and “Ne” was released in 2015. The project later developed from Da Davo’s solo format into a trio. Glenn Keteleer, also known as Radical G, joined the project during the 2010s, while Pieter-Jan Theunis joined on bass around 2014/2015. By the time of “Apollo”, the lineup was Dirk Da Davo on guitar and vocals, Glenn Keteleer on electronics and vocals, and Pieter-Jan Theunis on bass guitar. “Apollo” was released on April 12, 2019, through DanceDelic-D in co-production with Wool-E Discs. Neon Electronics also worked with Oráculo Records. “Mondriaan” was released as a limited vinyl EP in January 2019, ahead of “Apollo”. The project returned with a rework of The Neon Judgement track “Factory Walk” in December 2024, followed by “Nothing For Nothing” in July 2025 and “Justification Unknown” in February 2026. In 2026, Oráculo Records released “Liberation”, described by the label as “the final chapter in the journey of Dirk Da Davo”. The release featured Dirk Da Davo, Glenn Keteleer and Pieter-Jan Theunis, with remixes by Ancient Methods and Patrick Codenys of Front 242. The digital edition included eight tracks, while the limited 12-inch vinyl edition was pressed in 300 copies.

items.body: Brooklyn synthpop duo Observation Room have announced their debut album, “Superstructure”, set for release on 11 September 2026 through à La Carte Records. The duo of Marina F and Chloe Olson shared the record’s first single, “Running Lights”, in early July 2026, with pre-orders open at Bandcamp. “Superstructure” is the first full-length from Observation Room, following the self-titled EP the pair released in 2025. Marina F produced and mixed the album in Brooklyn, and Sharon Aiza Engel mastered it. Superstructure by Observation Room What Observation Room confirmed about ‘Superstructure’ The album pairs synthpop with drum programming and layered vocals from both members. Its reference points include Depeche Mode, OMD and Book of Love, along with the early Human League and krautrock. Marina F and Chloe Olson tie the lyrics to surveillance, social control and anxiety, connecting private tension to public systems. “Running Lights” is the album’s first single and its opening track, a steady, club-tempo piece led by Marina F’s production. A full tracklist for “Superstructure” has not been confirmed. The record keeps Observation Room on à La Carte Records, the independent collective that has released music by acts Side-Line has covered before, among them Julia Gaeta and Don’t Get Lemon. à La Carte is based in Los Angeles and Washington, DC. About Observation Room Observation Room began as the solo project of Marina F, a Brooklyn-based producer and vocalist who built the earliest demos while traveling between rural Maine and New York City. Chloe Olson later joined on bass, synthesizers and vocals, turning the project into a duo and filling out its live sound. The pair introduced Observation Room with the single “Workers”, then released their self-titled debut EP on à La Carte Records on 11 July 2025. The four-track EP – “The Face of the City”, “Workers”, “Orange Moon Distance” and “Semi-Precious” – was produced and mixed by Marina F in New York City and mastered by Will Killingsworth. à La Carte issued it on two vinyl variants, a blue and red splatter 12-inch limited to 50 copies and a natural 12-inch limited to 100, and the EP streams on Spotify, Apple Music, Bandcamp, Tidal and YouTube Music. The duo’s Bandcamp page also hosts an earlier set of recordings, “Can’t Feel a Thing (Collected Demos)”. With “Superstructure”, Observation Room move from a four-track EP to a full-length while keeping Marina F in the production seat and staying with à La Carte Records for their first album. The record arrives on 11 September 2026, led by “Running Lights”.

items.body: Texan artist Rona Rougeheart has been active as SINE for several years, releasing music on labels such as Re:Mission, Emergency Hearts, and Negative Gain Productions. With “La Mordre”, however, she takes a major step forward, marking her debut release on Metropolis Records. “La Mordre” is a captivating musical experience—one that stands out for both its originality and its consistently high quality. Rather than sounding like a derivative of better-known acts, SINE has developed a distinctive sonic identity all her own. Her music seamlessly blends elements of Minimal-Electro, Dark-Pop, Industrial, and even touches of Hip-Hop into a cohesive and compelling whole. The album is built around deep, resonant bass tones, slow and seductive rhythms, and Rougeheart’s semi-spoken, sensual vocal delivery. Together, these elements create an atmosphere that is both unsettling and intensely alluring, balancing darkness with an undeniable sense of intimacy. From beginning to end, “La Mordre” delivers one outstanding track after another. Its hypnotic grooves and provocative mood make it the perfect soundtrack for an underground fetish club or a late-night Industrial dancefloor. This is an album that dares to be different—and succeeds with remarkable confidence. (Rating:8½). SINE released “La Mordre” in May 2026, a ten-track album that gathers four earlier singles alongside six new recordings. Listen to “Succumb To Me”: Succumb To Me by SINE About SINE SINE is the solo project of Rona Rougeheart, a drummer, vocalist, producer, and multi-instrumentalist based in Austin, Texas. Rougeheart uses the term “Electronic Boom” to describe the project’s sound, which blends sub-bass, beats, and industrial elements with lyrics that incorporate sarcasm, humour, and social commentary. The project’s early releases appeared on Austin’s eMERGENCY heARTS label. SINE’s 2021 album “Desire, Denial and Paramania” was released on 7 October 2021 and featured collaborations with Curse Mackey, producer Sean Beavan (Nine Inch Nails, 3Teeth), and vocalist Chris Connelly (Pigface, Revolting Cocks). The album also included a Meat Beat Manifesto remix by Jack Dangers. In January 2022, SINE released a remix of “Attack” by Adrian Sherwood on eMERGENCY heARTS, and in August 2022 issued the EP “Mantis 2” on the same label. SINE signed to Metropolis Records ahead of the 2024 album “Luxuria”, released on 19 January 2024. That record was produced by Claus Larsen of Leæther Strip and included the single “From Beyond” featuring Leæther Strip. Over the course of her career, Rougeheart has collaborated with Adrian Sherwood, Meat Beat Manifesto, Clan of Xymox, Chris Connelly, Mark Pistel, Andee Blacksugar (KMFDM, Blondie), Xiu Xiu, and the late Mark Stewart of The Pop Group. “La Mordre,” her second Metropolis release, arrives roughly two years after “Luxuria” and marks a step into a longer, more expansive album format.

Ghost Dubs & The Bug duppy the latter’s cult, isolationist ambient excursion of 2022 with apposite measures of lead-boot trod and atmospheric levity for the hardest-to-please industrial dub freaks.

Selected cuts from ’Sub Zero’ - Kevin Richard Martin’s concerted return to interests in ambient-dub-noise fundamentals - are robustly togged out with bass insulation and Goretextured to the elements for a supremely crushing session that benefits from the biggest speakers you can lay yr mitts on. It catches KRM arguably in his imperial phase, sustaining a tear of substantial gear penned under his own name since ‘Sirens’ (Room 40, 2019) deep into the belly of his sound, to now clasp these chiral aspects of his steez - the supine, sunken, and strongback, stepping - in a deathly bind.

KMR’s key spar and Pressure MVP, Ghost Dubs goes super dank and wide on his half, opening subterranean caverns of space below ‘When I’m Gone’, punctuated only by abandoned ice-breaker clank and timber-shiver chorales, before pushing leagues below into knackered Porter Ricks or Rhythm & Sound terrain on rework of ‘Sorrow’. Martin keeps up his end of the bargain with a sonorous diffusion of ‘Screwed’, all icy plangency and keeling bass recalling aspects of Mika Vainio’s ‘Kilo’, then plumbing guttural crevasses of the spirit on remix of ‘Too Human’.

items.body:
Ana Roxanne’s gorgeous third album, one that finds her ditching the muted, Grouper-like ambience of her earlier work in favour of more sparse, exposed recordings and arrangements that come hugely tipped if yr into Eliana Glass, Susanna Wallumrød, Ethel Cain...

We called Roxanne's last Kranky outing, 2020's effervescent 'Because of a Flower', a "modern classic" - and 'Poem 1' is even stronger. Where its predecessor worked as a cryptonostalgic dream diary, sketching her various component parts - her early obsession with R&B, her introduction to Hindustani music, her life as a jazz hopeful and her college-era fixation on Alice Coltrane - into a surreal, multi-dimensional image, 'Poem 1' is a clean break, or at the very least the beginning of a new era. Her old influences still haunt the backdrop, but Roxanne's third album (if you count her brief but popular debut '~~~') is very much about the present, specifically the days and months that followed a breakup. Rather than wallow in self-pity, Roxanne uses the opportunity to reveal herself fully for the first time, stripping her music of its most tangible aesthetic signifiers to allow her voice to show its most affecting vulnerabilities. So there's no more looping and barely a lick of reverb, yet her voice still soars, accompanied by the simplest instrumentation.

She needs little more than a frozen string drone on 'The Age of Innocence' as she introduces herself again six years after the fact, not as broken pieces but a bold, unwavering voice that cuts through the noise (and pain) of existence. It's a revelation; the motivation has always been there in her music, hidden beneath the repetitions and gestures, and now we witness the fuller picture. "Wild wind blowing / A song playing over the air," she calls out on 'Berceuse in A-flat Minor, Op. 45', playing dimly-lit piano phrases as she sings. "Don't go, don't go." You can imagine being perched at the back of a lounge somewhere late at night, nursing a whiskey while watching Roxanne pour out her heart. Calling it Lynchian might be too close to the bone, but there's always been an air of Julee Cruise's haunted dream-pop hanging in the atmosphere and it wafts to the surface here, bathing Roxanne's words in blue light and stage smoke. "Oh I can never reach you / So I'll keep a piece beside me," she weeps solemnly on 'Keepsake'. "I'll hold it like a jewel, I'll carry the air." 

With these heartbreakers in the rearview, the album's centerpiece 'Untitled II' still hits like a brick to the jaw. Bohren-style doomed, jazzy drums brush away in the background and Roxanne's voice does all the emotional heavy-lifting at half speed. “Losing what I had," she sings, exacting a torturous look at the aftermath of a love lost. The piano and strings help lubricate the movement, but there's nothing to distract us from her words, punctuating them with sluggish, minor key stabs. Crushing and beautiful, it's one of the year's first unquestionable highlights - buy on sight, basically.

Returning after a 13 year absence, Boards of Canada's vision of hell isn't exactly surprising, swapping out the magic hour guitars of 'The Campfire Headphase' and the tired Carpenter-isms of 'Tomorrow's Harvest' for jagged distortions, dialog snippets and uneasy religious symbolism.

It can't be easy for Mike Sandison and Marcus Eoin; as soon as they cracked the code with 'Music Has the Right to Children' in 1998, their home-brewed signature sound - tape-warped, reverb-soaked monosynths, stuttering dialog samples and thumping MPC-breaks - became a sort of meme, regurgitated by a wave of bedroom musicians so frequently that the original references became fully hollow. Those early records were great because they sounded so unique, marking a landscape littered with post-'Chiastic Slide' crunches and choppy AFX-ian amens with new channels of thought. Just go back to their shadowy 'Twoism', 'Hi Scores', or that Mask 500 cover of 'Midas Touch' -  there was nowt else like it. By the time we got to 'The Campfire Headphase', a comparatively sunny, guitar-led misstep that arrived a few years later and then 2013's 'Tomorrow's Harvest' -  it all felt like diminishing returns.

'Inferno''s mysterious VHS rollout also felt overly familiar - and if you're gonna tease, the payoff best be worth it. Sadly, first single 'Prophecy At 1420 MHz' was damp and old fashioned, lumpen with boxy '80s drums and awkward prog rock synths - the signs didn't look good. Heard as a whole though, 'Inferno' hangs together pretty well. The brothers do a good job of laying out a vision of hell that's intricately connected to their well-worn source material: the lost future that was promised to wide-eyed 1970s kids raised on color TV, welfare and action figures. Back then, religious cults and street cranks were screaming of damnation, convincing weakened minds that judgement was coming while the Vietnam War raged - real hell was on the doorstep all along. And it's hard not to hear Boards' blend of seemingly old-fashioned religious symbolism (the Hare Krishna chants, chopped-up divinity school lectures and guided meditations) as an indirect reference to the wars raging right now. Certainly, it's their darkest album in years; not the aesthetic darkness of 'Tomorrow's Harvest', either. 'Father and Son', with its eerie Abrahamic symbolism, feels like an American Gothic reflection of Leslie Nielsen's comparatively benign narrations on 'Geogaddi', while 'Memory Death' feels like Boards actively sending off their own patented brand of hauntology with the EKG blip to prove it.

Throughout the record, BoC appear to juxtapose a cultural concept of hell with their own aesthetic responses, balancing dystopian robot voices with squelchy acid gurgles on the excellent 'The Word Becomes Flesh' and Bobby Beausoleil-style chiming strings on 'Blood in the Labyrinth'.  'The Process', meanwhile, offers a late-stage vision of aviation hell, a 'Langoliers'-style horror cue that neatly precedes the saccharine vintage BoC hit of 'You Retreat in Time and Space'. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it's these beatless moments that really hold things together - maybe they should have just leaned into it and done a full length of those vignettes. Still, 'Inferno' has its moments.

The second ever public performance by Nurse With Wound, captured on tape in 1984 and held in Steven Stapleton's archive across the four decades since, now available on a vinyl edition for the first time - every copy painted by hand, edition of 300.

You get the measure of this one with Steven Stapleton’s assertion that this was less a gig and more a “series of confrontations with audiences who often had no idea what they were watching.” which is basically everything we hope for watching pretty much anything.

It belongs to a moment when Stapleton, working alongside collaborators including David Tibet, Andrew McKenzie of The Hafler Trio, and a rotating cast of percussionists and string players, was carrying NWW briefly out of the studio. The performance moves through the territory NWW had been mapping across Homotopy to Marie and Nature Unveiled: long passages of pre-recorded tape collage assembled by Stapleton and McKenzie, ridden over by live electronics, voice, percussion, and a surreal theatrical instinct.

or as the band call it, “a collective groping”

aye.

One half of Rezzett, Jackson ‘Tapes’ Bailey reels off a lush new age ambient / environmental soundtrack primed for deep immersion, originally intended for his partner’s food sculpture exhibition at Gianni Manhattan Gallery, now thankfully shared with the rest of us via Good Morning Tapes.

No dub or dungeon synfs here: instead, just under an hour of spirit-purifying, Kankyō Ongaku x olfactory synaesthesia, using a palette of vaporous electronics to suggest rich aromas, tastes, and fleeting tongue-tip sensations. The palette is minimal and evocative, gliding from exquisite, gossamer-soft FM synths, to a more reverential mode, glazed in sacred motifs.

For sound-bathing dreamers and anyone into Hiroshi Yoshimura’s OG environmental templates - this one’s a doozie.

A decade since debuting as Ndagga Rhythm Force, Mark Ernestus’ incredible band draw on 100’s of hours studio and live practice for a staggering new suite of Senegalese x Berlin-styled mbalax steppers that prove, where needed, why they’re one of the best to do it right now. Absolutely exemplary, transcendent music for those that know.

Back at the start of the 2010s dub techno pioneer Mark Ernestus was spending a lot of time in Senegal, immersing in styles and patterns that historically underlined the reggae and dub musics he would heavily reference in his pivotal records made as Maurizio/Basic Channel/Rhythm & Sound, as co-produced with Moritz Von Oswald during the ‘90s and into the ’00s. 

In the process of researching and getting down to the roots of his passions, Ernestus encountered some of Senegal’s top tier musicians and recorded the Jeri-Jeri ensemble, revolving vocalist Mbene Diatta Seck and sabar drummer Bada Seck, and generating in 2013 the ‘800% Ndagga’ CD and its ’Ndagga Versions’ sibling, which better showcased Ernestus’ famed dub tekkerz inseparably woven into Senegalese music and the roots of myriad Afro-diasporic sounds.

That unit would morph into Ndagga Rhythm Force, producing an LP and trio of 12”s in 2015-2016 that set them on course to become one of the most impressive African bands on the contemporary gig circuit, throwing down live sets known to effortlessly go over 2 hours and propel so many legs and minds to new shapes and feels - trust they slay every time and should be top of all must-see lists.

With ‘Khadim’ Ndagga ditch their guitars and recalibrate a more lissom trio of voice and acoustic instruments bound with Ernestus’ Prophet 5 synth - the same model he’s relied upon since the Basic Channel days - on four extended songs that allow more light, space and emotion into a signature, rolling sound, centre-staging Mbene Seck’s husky diva croon over Bada Seck and Serigne Mamoune Seck’s dual, polymetric percussion, and judiciously juggled with Ernestus’ anti-gravity basses and plangent dub chord syncopation. 

In traditionally open-ended frameworks the quartet take all the time needed to stretch out and wrap heads into the tapestries of their storytelling grooves. A newfound atmospheric pressure and presence emerges in procession from the location recordings that fringe ‘Lamp Fall’ and its ode to a local mosque, reverberating in acres of implied space set by the ricocheting sabar drums and near-infrasonic subs, thru to the devotional depths of ’Nimzat’, rippling with thunderous chords and doleful ache. 

At its core are the LP’s most impressive parts; ‘Dieuw Bakhul’ uncoils a spellbinding Wolof tale of treachery to the rafters amid tempestuous chords that writhe stereo-wide with red-lining bite whilst drums knot sinuous, serpentine, to be resolved in the breathtaking 13’ steppers’ flight of ‘Khadim’, which lyrically hails Islam’s role in guiding Senegal to postcolonial times, spiritually meditates on bluest minor key riffs, and physically elevates bodies with aerodynamic finesse and hypnotic chronics kin to the best reggae and its offshoots. 

Deadly, soul and hoof gripping tunes. Do not miss!

Part 1 of a 12" series featuring Beatrice M.’s 'Sinking', the rudely aerodynamic debut LP where Tectonic's franco-british hope flexes a signature balance of ruff & smooth, building on a solid reputation earned via 12”s with her label, Bait, plus Tempa and Darwin’s SPE:C.​

Dubstep is not necessarily an album genre: beyond scant examples from the likes of Burial, Shackleton, or 2562, 12”s and DJ sets serve the sound in best context. However, Beatrice M.’s grasp of subtle sensuality and propulsive traction patently ends itself well to the format on ’Sinking’, with rolling, stepping and skanking permutations that deftly dance in the space between dubstep, proper, and its close-related cousins - UKG, broken beat, dub techno - with a finely measured proprioception of space, weight and pressure. 

Along with 2562’s recently dispensed ‘Lost Dubs 2006-09’, ’Sinking’ is arguably the best thing on Tectonic in recent memory, with a sound that revels in more ambiguous club suss. It’s the type of release primed for cans/buds as much as big cones, proving she’s equally adept at sublime tension, as in the languid ‘Ever’, as propelling a dance in the Martyn-esque wriggler ‘Motion’, and offbeat hood of ‘Disco Corner’.

items.body:
Taking their cues from the 1968 silent film 'Le Révélateur', Berlin-based Hungarian-Transylvanian artist Réka Csiszér (aka VÍS) and Radwan Ghazi Moumneh (aka Jerusalem in My Heart) use synths, voices and various instruments to breathe new life into Philippe Garrel’s iconic work.

If you heard last year's grimly romantic 'Danse des Larmes', Csiszér's second VÍS album and another one-of-a-kind oddity on the always good Heat Crimes label, you might already have an inkling of how good this one's gonna be. The record was made between November 2025 and February of this year between Zurich and Montréal, where Moumneh runs the legendary Hotel2Tango studio, and it's some of the most chilling material we've heard from either artist. The duo first met in 2018 and initially debuted their soundtrack to 'Le Révélateur' live in 2023; the film had been a long-time favorite of Moumneh's, but Csiszér didn't need much convincing - its themes of displacement and disorientation made immediate sense to an artist who'd grown up with an ever-shifting idea of home, born in East Germany before moving to Vienna.

And after performing their free-flowing soundtrack a handful of times, improvising within a set of tight themes, they decided to document the project properly, borrowing a mate's house in Montréal for a few weeks to record the meat and bones. And although the baseline for the album version of the collaboration is the same ("composed through improvisation," they say), it sounds as if the themes have been weathered and lived in a little at this stage. If you've seen the film, you'll realize it's the unique mood - accentuated by Garrel's stark lighting and Michel Fournier's bold black-and-white cinematography - that carries it, and it's this high-contrast, peripatetic motion that Csiszér and Moumneh capture so magically. 

Opening track 'wahid – واحد' suggests darkness ahead with its eerie environmental sounds (creaking gates, crackly vinyl, caged birds), scraped strings and isolated synths that accompany a shot of a couple smoking in a door frame, their silhouettes cut out of the sunlight. But like the film itself, it's the juxtaposition that makes it hit; 'ithnan – اثنان' is almost celestial, an uncanny hymn made from analogue drones and soft-focus wordless voices. And when they shift into grittier territory on 'arba'a – أربعة', a short distorted instrumental that sits alongside a shot of a young boy seemingly torturing a doll, the album's long centerpiece 'khamsa – خمسة' follows it up with Csiszér's most stunning vocal performance, that lifts a long shot of the nomadic family walking down a forest road.

It's minimal but never for dull for even a moment - best viewed alongside Garrel's film for the optimum experience.

Smacking that sweetspot between grime, techno, bassline and soca, Anthoney J Hart (East Man, Imaginary Forces) aka Basic Rhythm delivers a full-bore pack of rampers for Bristol-via-Berlin’s bassbin overlords, Sneaker Social Club.

Active in a vein of uchronic, ‘nuum-bending invention since the 2010’s, but with roots reaching back to ‘90s pirate radio, Hart’s decade-straddling steez yields the crankiest horsepower as Basic Rhythm on ‘8 Bar Techno’. Hewing hard to the brief, he dissects and recombines styles & patterns with a fiercely upfront quality, trampling on putative borders with a rudeboy alacrity that works a treat on up-for -it ‘floors.

The durable torsion of OG jungle tekno and its myriad derivations are twisted into tensile girders, variously splitting the difference between 4/4 grime and hard groove techno in ‘the title tune, or panel-beating sublow into rictus bashiness on ‘Weed Killer’, while firing killer rounds of vocal cuts including the dancehall-grime of ‘Vibez’ with NyNy, or electroid drill with Lyrical Strally and Eklipse.

Along with the precision-tooled rufige of ‘Kонец века’ with Moscow Legend, the mutant soca gallop o ‘Ice cold’, and diesel-fuelled grime-techno of ‘More Pricks than Kicks’, or the dive-bombing darkness of ‘The Deluge’, it’s a hard set for discerning 140BPM shotters, and surely one of Basic Rhythm’s deadliest.

items.body:
Produced by Neek and Jabu's Amos Childs (aka O$VMV$M), Manonmars' third album is syrupy suite of smoke-hazed recollections and free associated reflections set to decelerated, semi-rhythmic bumps, sluggish samples and cloudy drones. Sturdy biz FFO Ka, MIKE, King Vision Ultra or Coby Sey.

Manonmars' 2018 debut is one of those albums we still go back to periodically. It's that rare meeting of minds: a space for O$VMV$M to flex their production muscle and a scratchpad for London-based MC, painter and photographer Jack Martyn Richardson to sketch out his vision of England. And his experiences and impressions on 'Entertainment System' still feel chewable. "Goddess on my arm and both our phones got no service," he quips on 'Goddess'. "Acid is lysergic, psychedelic rock is Turkish." His rhymes aren't throwaway, they map out an underground that's very recognisable, shadowed by O$VMV$M's tuff, effective soundscapes - beats that reference trip-hop, ambient music, exotica and '70s movie soundtracks as much as they do US rap. On opener 'Flam3throw3r', Mars raps in double-time over shrill horns that blot out any trace of a beat; Neek and Childs sound as if they're relishing the negative space, adding chic sword swipes to a track that's got little else to do with the Wu Tang Clan. And even when a lumbering beat kicks in on 'Decathlon', flipping from downtempo to no-tempo in the final act, it sounds as if it's just there to assert O$VMV$M's commitment to slowness - Mars doesn't even seem to notice, rhyming casually but never losing his internal flow.

On 'Nasyua', his slurred expressions duck and weave around industrial whirrs and animalistic groans. "There was a time when I had flaws now I've adapted," he slurs. "I hit the zoot like Steve Zissou in 'The Life Aquatic' / then I dashed it, Christian Bale in a facemask on some Bat shit." Bristol mainstays Franco Franco and Dali de Saint Paul turn up to assist on 'Volcanic Shield', one of the album's most conventional bangers, led by O$VMV$M's skittering Surf Gang-like beats and morse code blips, and cold light's Birthmark lends his voice to 'Infinite', going bar for bar with Mars over Neek and Childs' soupy slackened funk. These moments are when 'Entertainment System' really shines, blaring out like an old tape on a busted in-car audio system. 'Firewater' takes the same approach, leaving Mars to do his best as snares are reformed into splashes alongside sultry stabs and sax from Brum-based sound artist Lorenzo Prati. "My bitch white, she can scuba dive and ice climb," he spits. "Put the drink down, I wasn't in my right mind." It's music that laughs through the tears - what could be more British than that?

items.body:
Topdown Dialectic’s solo debut bow on False Aralia rounds up over a decade of material in supremely elusive style & pattern - all rug-pulling rhythms and hallucinatory fractals wrapped up with proper, hyperreal frisson. Massive chef’s kiss FFO Vladislav Delay, Beatrice Dillon, Paperclip Minimiser, Purelink, Marc Leclair.

An artist keenly observed since initial gestures on /\\Aught in the early ‘10s, and throughout their cult LP trilogy for Peak Oil during 2018-2021; Topdown Dialectic has become a unique facet of C.21st dub electronics, adored for their grasp of diffused spatio-textural sorcery and wraithlike grooves. Anyone paying close attention to emergent sounds via Peak Oil and its False Aralia offshoot may have guessed at TD’s signature, watermarked imprint on the Borgesian Term EP of late ’25, which can now be confirmed as the work of one and the same Izaak Schlossmann; a photographer and producer patently in possession of heightened proprioceptions and a rewardingly patient approach to lushly dissociative sonification. In other words, he makes some of the sexiest electronic music out there - stuff that genuinely feels like it was made this century - and his latest practically leaves you kissing the sky thru its 80 minutes of lip-biting, skin tingling pressure. 

On 16 tracks timed at exactly 5 minutes each, we’re placed in the presence of suggestive sorcery, eliding unarchived material and jams in a unique ecology of oneiric physics. Never overtly showy or overblown, there’s nevertheless a staggering level of ingenuity and synaesthetic effect to its detailed construction and gaseous fractals resembling the LSD or DMT experience. The label themselves compare its nuance to “the flicker of a candle over a desk of drum machines in a Midwestern basement, or the “first blush of sunlight over a tiny campground as subwoofers creak in the distance”, which proves a perfectly poetic analog to its digitally-smudged refractions and tongue-tip spectral tumescence. 

Ultimately, it’s a singular pleasure to immerse the senses in Topdown Dialectic’s self-contained soundsphere, and never more substantially so than on ‘False LP A’. Longtime enthusiasts will surely recognise his skill in parsing salient aspects of Basic Channel x Rhythm & Sound, and their descendants in Vladislav Delay or Pole, reframing those templates in far more uncertain space with a real animist magick. Each work feels tangibly, ambiguously alive, breathing with dynamics and more voluminous, macro scales, and iridescent with voices and details that commands attentive listeners who will have a field day zoning in/out to its illusive, holographic projections and syncopated chronics.

items.body:
The crown jewel of German duo Donna Regina's pre-Karaoke Kalk run, 'Follow the Sea' laid out the template for their best known albums, muddling electro-pop with exotica, dub and lounge and inhabiting the liminal zone between Julee Cruise and Saint Etienne.

Regina and Günther Janssen had already released three albums before 'Follow the Sea' arrived, and it was around this time that their music had begun to creep beyond Germany's borders. Matthew Herbert had issued the title track on his Lowlife imprint, bumping it up with his own remix and within a couple of years, Donna Regina had been snapped up by Karaoke Kalk, where they remained for their next umpteen full-lengths. And although each album is more or less the same, there's no other band who makes music quite like this. Regina's voice sounds pitch perfect here, calling over Günther's Kraftwerk-inspired synths on the lengthy 'Jungle' and hissing across a cheeky sample of Aphex Twin's 'Alberto Basalm' on 'Something Happy'.

It's pop music, but the kind of low-key, literate pop that no longer exists, crafted by two heads who clearly love music so much that they've been exhaustively jotting down their findings since 1992. And it's the duo's lack of consistent boundaries that keeps us coming back; they're able to lurch from dubby Americana ('Follow the Sea') to d&b ('Smile') and then try on some ritualistic 'My Life in the Bush of Ghosts' percussive experimentation - and it all sounds as if it's coming from the same honest space.

items.body:
Airbrushed, subtropical, new age ambient-jazz from Jesse Peterson’s Maui-based project, given its highest profile platform to date on Amsterdam’s Music From Memory, and warmly advised to admirers of his regular spars, Carlos Niño, Laraaji, Mia Doi Todd...

"Originally formed in New York in the late 2000s, Turn On The Sunlight has evolved into a fluid, location-spanning practice rooted in collaboration, intuition and process. Now based on Maui, Peterson’s work draws together a wide network of musicians and environments, with recordings taking shape across Los Angeles, Tokyo, London, San Miguel de Allende and Haʻikū.

Loosely situated within a framework of organic, ambient-leaning jazz, 'Iseo' unfolds as a series of open, exploratory pieces, with electronics sitting subtly beneath acoustic and environmental elements. Built from layered instrumentation including synthesizers, guitar, zither, flutes, voice and field recordings, Peterson moves between grounded, tactile detail and more expansive, immersive states. A sense of warmth and permeability runs throughout: organic percussion, environmental textures and drifting rhythmic elements lend the record a gently saturated humidity, reflecting Peterson’s base in Hawaii, where the presence of nature is felt as much as it is heard.

Underlying the project is a way of working rooted in gathering, listening and tending. Instruments, ensemble sessions, field recordings and everyday environments are approached with attentiveness, shaped through collecting, refining and allowing things to settle. Relationships, landscape and lived experience shape the sound, giving 'Iseo' a tactile, almost hand-made quality.

Rather than fixed arrangements, the album feels as if it has been organically and lovingly assembled through a process of listening and response, each element finding its place within a wider, evolving whole. This approach reaches a natural centre point in the 15-minute piece 'Medianoche En La Calle Aurora', which unfolds patiently, bending through shifting environments as motifs and textures emerge and dissolve with quiet continuity.

Peterson’s role as both instigator and facilitator is central to the project. Bringing together a diverse group of collaborators including Carlos Niño, Mia Doi Todd, Laraaji, Ko Ishikawa, Luis Pérez Ixoneztli and Miles Spilsbury, he creates space for individual voices to emerge within a shared language. The result is a music defined by openness and generosity.

'Iseo' takes its title from Peterson’s son’s middle name, a word that can be understood to mean ‘one-world life’. The piece itself takes the form of a gentle lullaby, its melody loosely shaped around the syllables of his name and sung to Peterson’s son by Luis Pérez Ixoneztli, a close collaborator whose presence across the record reflects a long-standing relationship that extends beyond the music itself.

Sleeve art and design by Michael Willis."

Hot on the heels of their ‘Junglist!’ set, Soul Jazz reload their anthem-studded 2007 comp, packing early-mid ‘90s hardcore and ragga jungle heat by M-Beat & General Levy, Ragga Twins, SUAD, Cutty Ranks x DJ SS.

‘Rumble In The Jungle’ tells the story of jungle’s rapid evolution from mutant hip hop x dancehall in the late ’80s, via hardcore, to its hugely distinctive ragga and jump-up phase of the mid ‘90s. It’s a baga sounds that successive waves of producers have attempted to emulate ever since, but simply doesn’t get better than the OG tackle, as Soul Jazz well know.

The Ragga Twins understandably dominate the set with three bullets, the foundational, acid dancehall rap of ‘Ragga Trip’, sped-up fast rap steez of ‘Illegal Gunshot’, both from 1990, plus the ragga techno of ‘Tan So Back’ (1992), which all sparks so many dances and imaginations BITD. Shut Up and Dance, who issued all the above, are also on board, but with the gummy 2000 garage of ‘No Doubt’, which is hardly a standard, but does show how the sound had muted 10 years later.

The rest is all dead solid as a primer for inquisitive junglists/junglettes, firing General Levy’s alternative national anthem ‘Incredible’ and the murderous DJ SS remix of Cutty Ranks’ ‘Limb By Limb’, beside lesser known but wicked zingers such as DJ massive’s clattering hardcore rufige in ‘Final Conflict’, a deep fried steppa by The Source, and of course X Project’s deadly ramp of Beenie Man & Barrington Levy’s ‘Under Mi Sensi’.

Following Kuboraum's eccentric 2024 first volume, the Berlin-based eyewear brand and occasional label returns with another broad-minded statement of intent featuring some of the contemporary avant-garde's most visible figures, including Low Jack, bela, Richie Culver, Rainy Miller, EROS, Lucrecia Dalt, Lee Gamble, Ziúr and Significant Other.

The set opens on a wheezing, spitting and growling loosie from bela, whose sorely overlooked 'Korean Love Sonnets' full-length is still fueling our nightmares. From there, we stay locked into the outerzone with Kuboraum vet Cosimo Damiano, an Italian techno mainstay who's veered off path in recent years, hitting SUPERPANG with his modular experiment 'Multi-Species' and helming that killer Salò record from 2023. On 'Copper Disk' he conducts an unsettling ritual, shifting voices until only ghostly outlines remain and setting the stage for similarly strong voice experiments from Marina Herlop and the unstoppable Lord Spikeheart.

Prolific French producer Low Jack shifts the mood when he invites Le Diouck to help out on the grimy, groove-fwd 'TLC' and the motion is oddly maintained by Romain Azzaro's trap-gamelan hybrid 'Fusion' and Richie Culver's rainy 'C-SIDE', that sounds as if it could have slipped off his Fixed Abode debut 'I TRUST PAIN'. What keeps us gripped here though is that while 'Kuboraum Sound Residency Vol. 2' keeps reinventing itself, it carries a similar energy throughout, an air of glam, oily darkness that links Significant Other's grinding 'Lust On Your Shoulders' with EROS's menacing 'Burnt Crossing' and Emiliano Maggi's tape dubbed lullaby 'Fury'. Even a long "refurbished" version of Ziúr's 'Home' LP title track featuring cellist Martina Bertoni and Subtext's Sara Persico sounds as if it's been repainted in Kuboraum's distinct color scheme: darkened significantly, but just so the edges stand out more than ever before.

Nkalipho Andile Mkhize aka Akiid blazes thru with 11 sharp sidespins on gqom, ama & Afrotech, inflected with Jersey club, trance, trap and techno - all demonstrating why he’s one of Durban’s rising stars.

‘Skeffu’ hustles some of the hottest strains of harder-edged club and street rave emerging from South Africa in the mid 2020s. The distinct sound speaks to Akiid’s peripatetic youth, moving between Durban townships where he picked up myriad local styles and patterns which fed into his rudely mutable and robustly disciplined sound. Call it gqom 2.0, hybrid Afrotech, or the Future Sound of Durban; whatever, it’s properly effective dance music certain to catch fire far beyond the source.

Fierce from front to back, ‘Skiffu’ is emblematic of the way SA artists absorb virulent sounds into their very particular dance vernacular. A youthful zeal for the thrills of contemporary Black Atlantic sounds - Jersey club, ATL trap, Chi & LDN drill - is factored by production techniques from megadome EDM, dub techno and even psytrance, to generate a ceaseless FWD traction in its pointed limb/limbic triggers. It’s all there in the breathless tension of ‘Chuck Norris’ and most impressive on the sound design staging of ‘MoonWalk Two’, where Jersey drill-type bass and an almost Burial-esque woodblock ushers detuned, mentasm-like licks to a heart-in-mouth breakdown.

As with any style, it’s possible to reach a point of saturation or exhaustion before the ears reach overfamiliarity and seek new thrills, and its maybe fair to say gqom hasn’t offered all that much that’s new in recent times (or at least that we’ve caught on to). But Akiid’s lust for fresh pressure, as heard on the angler canter of the title track, or his chimeric Jersey club x trance stabbed with isiZulu calls and scratch motifs in ‘Emotional Damage’, acutely remedy that issue with a thrilling, recombinant sense of club dramaturgy.

TIP!

A second pressing of last year’s gorgeous fourth and final album from Old Saw, the American Primitive project of Tongue Depressor's Henry Birdsey, riffing on the classic Takoma paradigm with additional ferric washes and layered instrumental drones, huge recommendation if yr into Bruce Langhorne’s ‘The Hired Hand’ or classic work by Daniel Lanois, Laraaji, Pelt, Stars Of The Lid, State River Widening.

'The Wringing Cloth' is Birdsey’s fourth and final Old Saw outing, and ironically it’s also the one that has garnered most amount of critical and commercial success. Old Saw’s shimmering, drone-heavy soundscapes were recorded on 1/4" tape at various locations in New England over the last few years and are once again paired with evocative black and white imagery from photographer Dylan Hausthor, whose landscapes somehow perfectly capture the timeless, widescreen appeal of the music inside.

Birdsey's pedal, lap steel and resonator are at the core of each track, but the album also features Old Saw’s usual personnel; Harper Reed on nylon string guitar and banjo, Ira Dorset on fiddle and bowed strings, Ann Rowlis on reed organ and harmonium, Jim Cutler on telecaster, Addison Starkweather-Price on bass, and Peter Catchpole on metal objects and power hammer. That lap steel lends the music its stylistic anchor, taking us through decades of American folk before gently fraying at the edges. Birdsey's application of classical minimalism - the themes that surge through his work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor - is still somehow present here, especially as the record pulls into its second side and the shimmering country-fied atmosphere is pierced with bell-like sounds, but the overall mood and flavour of the record is distinctly easy on the ear and timeless in its appeal.

As the label put it, “What has always been uncanny about this music is that it arrives in a state at once familiar and obscured, like a memory weighed down with sensory information but no identifying details to place it. The Wringing Cloth walks off further into that geographical dream without time or language, until it’s just a speck of light….”

Contours follows up an excellent LP for Music From Memory in 2024 with a strong  EP of percussive fancies, full of emotive Motor City pads x resonant drums, tipped FFO Dan Curtin, Workshop, Theo P, early Andy Stott, Gábor Lázár.

Cumbria-raised, Manchester-based Tom Burford’s Contours project was last heard on that Music from Memory ace transitioning into a more contemplative sphere with results comparable to Steve Reich, Richard Skelton, or Alice Coltrane. The 4 tracks here were recorded at around the same time as that LP, but follow an altogether more club-focussed trajectory, most successfully on ‘Sterile Light’ that features a square bassline that mimics Theo P's ‘Heal Yourself and Move’, except with stretched, plastic strings that could have been lifted straight off a theo burt record.

In other words, high praise!

items.body:
Balinese gamelan master Dewa Alit's third Black Truffle outing, 'Baur Bentur' continues to shake up the formula like it's a margarita, placing Alit's Gamelan Salukat ensemble alongside virtuoso jazz pianist Sri Hanuraga.

With each of Alit's Black Truffle albums, his first releases outside of Indonesia, the performer, composer, instrument designer and bandleader has projected Balinese gamelan forms into bold new places. 2020's 'Genetic' set the scene, introducing his orchestra and his uniquely tuned scale and its follow-up, 2022's 'Chasing the Phantom' considered gamelan's immense influence on electronic music, centering some of Alit's most experimental material. On 'Baur Bentur', which means "mixing and smashing", Alit again looks at the push-and-pull between East and West, this time wondering how to work out a fusion that's progressive, not something formulated around the gaze of parasitic tourists. He invites Jakarta-born Hanuraga to help him realize this goal and its a sensible choice; considered one of Indonesia's most talented young pianists, Hanuraga understands both avant-garde jazz and traditional Indonesian music implicitly. 

His playing is measured but ornate on 'Sukat Tacara', played in fast flurries of notes that recall gamelan without mimicking the form. It allows Alit's ensemble to take a different approach, laying down hollow rhythms at first and slow chimes before speeding up into more traditional overlayed, lightning-fast tones in the middle section. And it's at this moment that Hanuraga really steps into the spotlight, playing jerky Thelonius Monk-style sequences that mutate seamlessly into cascading gamelan riffs. The title track on the flip takes a different approach again, integrating Hanuraga's piano more holistically into the ensemble, where it follows the gamelan's rhythmelodic thrust absolutely, adding emphasis, accent and intrigue to a sound that's already exceptionally singular.

items.body:
Performed by Balinese gamelan duo KADAPAT and Indonesian singer and musician Nova Ruth Setyaningtyas, 'Ocean Cage' is a live recording of Asiandopeboys latest performance 'Moyang & Seaman', a collaboration with choreographer Siko Setyanto that draws from Japanese Noh theater and Nusantara traditions.

If you've been paying attention, you'll already know that anything with Tianzhuo Chen's name on it is worthy of a closer look. And Chen is in the director's chair on 'Ocean Cage', fusing installation art, choreography, live music and scenography into a brand new Asiandopeboys theatrical extravaganza that's almost predictably ambitious. The show is pegged to a narrative that's inspired by Indonesian whaling traditions and local legends, focusing on three characters that Setyanto interprets to build an allegorical account of displacement and ecological collapse. But the interesting part for those of us who aren't able to check into one of the shows is that the music is gripping even without the visuals; KADAPAT approach gamelan traditions with a refreshing level of irreverence, using electronic instruments as well as the traditional bamboo and metal tools to mash up the timeline, not exactly fusing gamelan elements with far-off templates but rethinking the form in situ. 

Their tonal clusters and rhythmic experiments are aptly meshed with Nova Ruth's powerful vocals, that sail across the soundtrack, sometimes squeezed into an unsettling robotic moan and oftentimes left to soar on its own. She grew up in Java and spent seven years traveling on the solar-powered boat Arka Kinari, a "floating cultural platform to sound the alarm on climate change." So the music sounds as if it's plugged into a reality that gets more stark each year; there's a sense that 'Ocean Cage', although it's steeped in ancient traditions, is being beamed from the future, a warning of where the world is headed if we don't do something immediately. It's beautiful, of course, but it's sobering too.

items.body:
Following her acclaimed 2022 album 'Weather Alive', Beth Orton returns with another fully self-produced collection of songs, this time bringing in help from Shahzad Ismaily, Vernon Spring's Sam Beste, drummers Chris Vatalaro and Vishal Nayak, trumpet player Christos Styliandes and bassist Tom Herbert.

Orton sounded refreshed on 'Weather Alive'. Taking the production into her own hands for the first time, she crafted a personal world that was completely her own, weaving in old recordings of her parents and recording a busted piano she snapped up at Camden Market. The music felt like a form of catharsis, dreamily reflecting on years of boozing and raving, when she made her mark as a guest vocalist for artists like the Chemical Brothers and William Orbit. That mature, knowing air - the kind of mettle you build up only after real-world experience - hangs around 'The Ground Above', giving Orton's tender, heartfelt songs genuine power and proper weight. When she sings "I'm as invincible as grief, dancing cross a lake of loss," on the epic opener 'The Ground Above', you don't doubt her for a moment.

Orton's voice has always been distinct, a soulful rasp that's fragile one moment and sturdy the next, and it sounds as if she's finally found the right music to match it. On that eight-minute opener, it's quick syncopated drums that lodge themselves somewhere between Roni Size's 'New Forms' and Radiohead's 'Hail to the Thief', reversed, psychedelic guitar riffs, jazzy horn blasts and pillowy ambient textures. 'Cigarette Curls', meanwhile, slows things down, pairing her voice with smudged piano phrases and smoke-y rhythms. She breezes past the shape of classic soul pop on 'Waiting', even taking on a half-sung chorus, but sounds most comfortable when she strips down the instrumentation even further, crooning over brushed percussion and euphoric pads on the gorgeous 'I'll Miss You'.

Will Long dons his dancing slippers for another deep house sojourn on his Long Trax Productions, blowing kisses in the direction of Larry Heard, Ron Trent, DJ Sprinkles.

One decade since minting the ‘Long Trax’ series on Terre Thaemlitz’s label, Comatonse, Will Long slow cooks six new additions on his personal folio, taking all the time needed to get right into the groove. Trust there’s no fireworks or over-produced trickery, just hypnotic deep house that unfurls with a real sense of space, patience and deferred gratification.

Long in his element, following his nose to pair the barest ingredients in classic style and pattern, as with with the likes of ‘About Where It's At (Now You Went N' Did It mix)’, which takes over 4 mins happily swinging away before introducing its lonesome flute motif, or a standout ‘Have to Have Something’ lost in the flow, where the bassline only thickens as it goes along. 

We’re also partial to the square bass budge of ‘Have To Have Something (S' a Lotta Shade mix)’, and the mesmerising meld of creamy bass and piquant cowbell pinging on ‘The Problems’, also found warped with trippier effect on its Metallic Dub reshape.

alias Junior Rain are the duo of sound poet Francesco Cavaliere and sound artist Matteo Martino, minting Turin’s Isotopes Records with a tape of exquisitely heatsick wooze tipped FFO Spencer Clark, Jan Jelinek, Lieven Martens, NWAQ, Actress, Rezzet...

‘Capello di Cristallo’ could hardly be a more fitting soundtrack to the head-melting heatwave right now. For just shy of 30 mins, Cavaliere dials down his signature sound poetry to instrumental form, matched by Matteo Martino’s ear for textural, world-building detail, as previously revealed on his tape for ace DIY label Canti Magnetici. Across 11 works, the duo transcend the sum of their influences; whiffs of rearview vaporwave and new age ambient entwine around impulses from lo-fi Midwestern house, and its Euro offshoots, in a treacle-thick air oozing with ferric wow & flutter that sounds custom-made for high heat.

Subtly distinguished from Cavaliere’s decades of work by its slow burning rhythms, the album sways to its own dreamy pace thru pieces that melt into one another. The silvery chord bursts and busted drums of ‘in discesa’ feel like a knackered Sun Ra, and ‘espansione’ incurs Raul Lovisoni & Francesco Messina’s Cramps touchstone, hinting at a spiritual ambient jazz freeness that also colours their titular vacillation of lo-fi house, and the Rezzett-esque romance in ‘junior rain’ or ‘ragnelata magica’. 

Consider it a compliment to the artists that if you reach the end of the spool in an eyes-half-closed, bezonked state, their work here is done.

A parody of Brian Eno's 'Music for Airports' recorded at the heart of a banana plantation in Tenerife, Lagoss's 'Música para Plátanos' (music for bananas) is anything but background music, fixing up its ratcheting polyrhythms and "Latin-infused electronics" with flimsy exotica and oddball environmental recordings.

The music of 'Música para Plátanos' isn't just about the plantation, it attempts to live, breathe and exist just like the bananas themselves, reacting to each element whether it's the temperature or the nourishment. And the tracks came together over weekly improvised sessions recorded over the space of five years, where the trio of Gonçalo F. Cardoso, Mladen Kurajica and Daniel Baez tapped into their groove, fusing samples and tape loops with shifting percussive forms, instrumental outbursts and radio interference. If you heard 2024's 'Plátano Tapes', you'll have a good idea where the source of this record came from, but that collage has been worked into, shaved down, shaped and refined since then, distilled as a "greatest rotten hits" according to the press release, for an album that's meant to be distinct from their ongoing 'Imaginary Island Music' series.

It's good stuff, too, more engaging than you'd expect from a collection of jams, but then Lagoss are a force to be reckoned with. There's horizontal exotica - the organ-led 'Mundo Sour' and the skittering 'Plata no Police' - and plenty of oily ambient biz (just check 'Milliones de Gallinas'), but Lagoss are best when they're in a percussive groove. On 'Mosca Blanca / Horcón Girl', they muddle field recordings with low-slung bassy grooves and circuitous island rhythms, and 'Plátano Saki' is Tenerife in dub, a banana-themed, sun-bleached anthem that's seasoned with tape echo, reverb and manic Lee "Scratch" Perry-esque oscillations.
