Referencing Van Dyke Parks, Robert Wyatt and Jim O'Rourke, Los Angeles' Aaron MF Olsen goes full chamber pop on his second "songs for singing" album.

Olsen keeps himself busy. In the last few years, he's penned a raft of scores (including one for Matt Hewitt's bizarre b-movie 'Hoagie'), worked alongside Jeff Parker and interpreted Mexican singer-songwriter José Alfredo Jiménez's classing songs on synthesizer. And he's also written two albums of proper songs: 2021's acclaimed 'Songs Album' and this impressive sequel, that's comprised of 10 well sculpted baroque pop moments, each one fleshed out by Olsen's band.

He's not quite as ambitious as Cindy Lee or Panda Bear, but there are moments when Olsen shows a similar command of past, present and future. As the throwbacky 'Nobody Can Tell' fades out, 'There Comes A Time' enters the frame in a brush of looped noise and synth euphoria before settling into its groove, and 'Who Do You Think You Are I Am?' is a minimal throb of staccato percussion and detuned piano hits that rights itself mid-way through when it transforms into a low-slung doo-wop anthem.

Capturing an in-situ rehearsal of The Sterling Jubilee Singers, a long-running African American a cappella quartet, 'Jesus Hits like the Atom Bomb' provides an intimate view of a dying folk tradition.

We should all know by now the foundational influence African American gospel music has had on subsequent popular forms, from country to house, but we rarely get to hear the real thing. This set was produced by the Alabama Folklife Association and aimed to document the rigorous process the Sterling Jubilees went through each week to maintain their notoriously high level of activity. The group was formed way back in 1929 from African American miners and mill workers in Birmingham, Alabama, and 'Jesus Hits...' catches up with them in 1994 in a hall that serendipitously sat next to a railway line. And whether you have any interest in OG gospel a cappella music or not, it's fascinating to hear the quartet in their element, praying in-between recreating their elaborate (and impeccably sung) set of standards. It's a porthole into another universe, for those of us who grew up far from the American South.

items.body:
Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less

items.body:
Abstract dub dream-weavers SKRS INTL. & WZRDRY remerge at the behest of Bristol’s Accidental Meetings for a super lush dose of wormholing ambient dance pressure tipped FFO Rezzett, Peak Oil/False Aralia, Second Woman.

‘Orbit Flares’ combines the two Canadian units for the first time in over a decade, naturally reprising an empathic level of vibes in a half hour of music that betrays illusive tekkerz developed over the interim. Any semblance of sharp edges are smudged to a brilliantly psychedelic, polychromatic lustre and laced with disciplined, yet properly wayward rhythms that tumble, buckle and vaporise in fractious delirium. Each new SKRS drop is welcome around ours but, jeez, they really push into their most impressive work here, possibly thanks to wzrdryAV’s synaesthetic suss.

Front to back it feel likes they catch minds/bodies in the split second before going under anaesthesia, and extrude us into pitch-bent helical vortices of plonging dub chords and gooey bass, finding bold new realms of computerised dub suss. Handrails are slippery as fuck, ground melts beneath feet, leaving bodies gyring in space between the weightless dub techno inflections of ‘1.1’, into air-stepping chicanery on ‘1.2’, or glitching like a hair-kissing Vladislav Delay on ‘1.3’. The smeared chords and scudding subs of ‘2.1’ call to mind Second Woman emulating the illusive dub-soul of False Aralia drops, and ‘2.3’ feels like distant rig heard on a Nitrous-induced permo. 

Sheer class for harder to please future dub freaks.

items.body:
Featuring MØ, Quiet Light, Koilwood, Helena Gao and others, Copenhagen duo A Good Year's second album is another slick set of trip-hop inspired Danish pop from the reliable Escho stable, home of Smerz, Astrid Sonne, Iceage and Snuggle.

Albert Hildebrand and Tobias Laust Hansen didn't have a fixed idea in mind when they started work on 'Play'. As the title suggests, it emerged from just playing, improvising with each other and shuttling recordings back and forth between their collaborators. "The music became a vessel for connection," they explain. "A way to reach to people we admire, but also a way to create a social element within these sometimes introverted jams." And their approach leads to an uncommonly light set of almost-pop; it's still as neatly polished as anything from the fertile Copenhagen scene, but there's a willing naivety that allows breathing room, a way for errors to slip in and humanize the material in the face of AI perfection.

Fine collaborator Koilwood shows up on the charming 'Back of a car', whispering softly over Hildebrand and Hansen's skipping lo-fi beats and skeletal instrumentation and Tiffi Malmgren lends her voice to early highlight 'Flight', a slo-mo trip-hop dream that's lifted by the duo's tape-warped piano vamps and hazy textures. And Malmgren returns with Major Lazer collaborator MØ (yep it was her on 'Lean On') on the album's stand-out 'Blue Flame', an electrified indie anthem that makes good use of the Danish singers' unique, recognizable voices. Scandi pop lovers, this'll hit the spot.

items.body:
Released in 2017, Dasein was Richard H. Kirk's first solo album in 5 years, recorded by the founding member of Cabaret Voltaire at Western Works, Sheffield, over a three-year period.

"Work began with recording on midi and analogue synthesisers before guitar and vocals (Kirk’s first use of vocals in 10 years) were added. Kirk explains, “A lot of time was spent on post-production, editing and then living with the material and I think it benefited from stepping back and then revisiting after doing other things.”

Although not an overtly political album, it’s hard not to hear a reaction to recent years’ world events in the overwhelming urgency of ‘Nuclear Cloud’ or ‘20 Block Lockdown’ or in ‘New Lucifer / The Truth Is Bad’. When questioned Kirk admits, “It’s not really a political album, but over recent years – during the recording – all manner of horrorshow events have cropped up and now we seem to be in a rerun of the Cold War with Russia back as the Bogeyman.” The album’s title, Dasein (a German word meaning “being there” or “presence”, often translated into English as “existence”), is a fundamental concept in existentialism.

Kirk explains “culture succumbs to nostalgia in much the same way that an individual looks back wistfully to adolescence or childhood - the nostalgia is partly for a time when he or she wasn’t nostalgic, just lived purely IN THE NOW.” In 2014, during the recording period, Kirk began work on Cabaret Voltaire live and so the two projects coexisted in tandem. Although Kirk’s varied projects have always existed separate to one another, says Kirk, “in the past some solo works served as a blueprint for what I did later with Cabaret Voltaire”.

Billed as a performance consisting solely of machines, multi-screen projections and Richard H. Kirk, Cabaret Voltaire recently announced the first UK performance in over 20 years at the Devil’s Arse Cave (aka Peak Cavern) in Castleton, Derbyshire on Saturday 29 April. Kirk will perform entirely new material for a performance relevant to the 21st Century with no nostalgia."

100% killer reissue of Bim Sherman’s self-released 1988 dub masterpiece ‘Ghetto Dub’, mixed by King Tubby, Prince Jammy and Adrian Sherwood who diffuse rhythms by The Roots Radics and Sly & Robbie, newly remastered for its first new edition in 30 years.

With 2nd hand prices understandably climbing into triple figures, this overdue first vinyl reissue will be mana to the fiends. It takes pride of place in an ongoing programme of resurrected Sherman aces to portray him at his most elusive and atmospheric, or as the hype sticker calls it, “a journey in echo and space”.

His legendarily tone is threaded thru the desk by a team of JA/UK titans with the man himself in the producer role, sifting cuts from his Century Records: a label set up in the Uk in 1984, after his move from Kingston, JA, to London, where he became a crucial figure in the On-U Sound crew after joining their 1979 tour, and would lend to classic Dub Syndicate cuts among others. 

The record’s renown has grown over the years since Sherman’s passing in 2000 and the effective dissolution of his label. Week-End Records now do a sterling job of preserving his legacy with this edition, richly representing the warmth and pressure of the OG in its entirety, from the clean-spurred, buoyant step of its title tune to moon-booted ‘Untitled Dub’, via the soul-tugging ace ’Station Dub’ with its unanswered doorbells, and best showcase of his voice in ‘Moving Dub’, another alright stepper in ‘World Dub’, the bloozy wooze of ‘Danger Dub’ and wickedly skewed Afro-lilt of ‘Tribulation Dub.’

All killer.

items.body:
Drawing on his experiences in Ghana, Niamké Désiré approaches his third record with a different energy, infusing his productions with noise and chaos to offset the fragile beauty of his work with violinist ASIA. RIYL Kevin Martin, Tim Hecker, Shapednoise or Ben Frost.

Describing his recent trip to Ghana as "an overwhelming, magnificent organization of noise," Désiré returned to Paris determined to shake up his methodology. He's already proven himself on albums like 2021's 'Simulacrum', 2023's 'Rhizomes' and last year's 'Ego Death' collaboration with Resina to be a prodigious sound designer and deep thinker, but he realised that it was stepping outside of his head that was needed. So, thinking about the journey rather than the destination, Désiré began to work on music with violinist ASIA for a Parisian commission that was more assertively personal, considering the actual feeling of "diasporic in-betweenness" he experienced as he moved between Paris and Ghana, rather than speculating on philosophy. The result was '100 Soleils', a lengthy composition that Désiré splits into four pieces on 'The Sun Turned Black', using it as a blueprint for the feel of the entire record. 

Threaded through with ASIA's delicate string work, Désiré's newfound confidence in noise evolves over the course of almost half an hour, giving Désiré's competent sound design the fangs it needed. There's natural chaos to the soundscape he creates on '100 Suns, Pt. II', animalistic screeches that complement his digitally-shaped elements, and we begin to sense an interplay between very different worlds. Désiré creates the same friction between the electronic and acoustic instrumentation, building vast artificial melodic structures on the towering '100 Suns, Pt. III' and resolving them on the fourth chapter with ASIA's sweeping strings. Breaking up the piece, 'The Children of Noise' establishes dissonance and the title track acts as a brief, gratifying conclusion, finding harmony between the desiccated, buzzing noise and Désiré's richly textured harmonic clouds.

items.body:
'Aeternum (Existenz)' from Dave Sumner, aka Function on Tresor. 

"Much like the fusion resulting in the output of light and heat within a star, the last seven years for Dave Sumner, aka Function, have been defined by immense change and an outpouring of creative energy. What began in late 2016 as a period of burnout from a relentless touring life became a catalyst for the most prolific recording era of his career. At the time, the studio became the only viable escape, a space to transmute exhaustion into a gestalt work.

Aeternum (Existenz) serves as the missing element in this creative arc. It acts as the final chapter of a cycle, that began with the 2019 album Existenz and moved through Subject f (Transcendence), Awakening from the Illusory Self, and Green EP. Drawing inspiration from the seven stages of alchemy, this mini-album represents a cathartic process; a natural end point of a psychological cycle and the beginning of a new curve.

Across the six tracks on the mini-LP, recorded 2016-2019, Function builds a unique world, one which underlines his place as one of the luminaries of contemporary techno.

Opening track, Ascent, traverses the space between ambient and techno; second track City Of Luz almost fades into itself across its twelve minutes before Transmutation brings around a reawakening with a beat that would not have sounded out of place on an early Rephlex or even a Sähko release. Final track on the 12”, Growth Cycle is fittingly a re-version/re-vision of a track on the Existenz LP; Robert Owens’ soulful vocal now Stefanie Parnow's floating Siren-like voice with music that feels reborn: fresh, strong and insistent.

The digital pack contains two further tracks, the deep electro of November 29, as well as Rubedo, a spacial ambient track that feels like the final glowing red embers of a fire turning to ash as the sun rises to reveal a new, golden dawn.

Aeternum (Existenz) is the final chapter of the soundtrack to Function’s spiritual awakening, the closing of a door and the clearing of a path. It’s a sonic manifestation of the Magnum Opus completed, a moment of total integration, where the leaden weight of the journey is finally perfected into the incorruptible gold of the spirit.

It is dedicated to John Mendez, aka Silent Servant, Sumner’s dear friend and lifelong collaborator."

In their sublime duo debut the simpatico synth & guitar of Jonny Nash & Tomo Katsurada is seduces to blissed, wind-whispering soundscapes, hashed out over the course of 12 months since Katsurada lent strings to Nash’s ‘Once Was Our Forever’. Dream material FFO Ghost, Makoto Kawabata, Joanne Robertson...

"Netherlands-based artists Tomo Katsurada (Ex-Kikagaku Moyo / Future Days Radio) and Jonny Nash (Melody As Truth) combine forces for an exploration into the sonic potential of the guitar duo, rooted in their experiences performing together over the last 12 months.

Friends and admirers of each other’s work for a decade, their musical collaboration began in 2024 with Katsurada asking Nash to contribute guitar to his debut EP ‘Dream Of The Egg’. Sensing the need to explore this further, they spent the following year performing together in different configurations, with Nash joining Katsurada’s trio and Katsurada in turn playing with Nash as a duo, across a wide spectrum of spaces, from churches and temples to concert halls, theatres and outdoor festivals. With new ideas developing organically out of these performances, recording new material became the next logical step. A short period of three days was set aside with a clear goal: to capture the essence of their fluid, intertwining melodies and guitar playing in a way that felt as direct and unfiltered as possible. Working from a handful of pre-existing sketches, they left ample room for experimentation to unfold within the process.

The results are presented on ‘At The Emerald Pool’, a collection of ten pieces that offer the listener a full immersion into the pair’s sound. With guitar as the primary instrument for both artists, it is no surprise that the core of the album lies here, specifically in the fluid interplay between the two players. Layers of gentle, delay-soaked fingerpicking often make it almost impossible to distinguish where one player ends and the other begins. As soloists, both Katsurada and Nash have a gift for crafting melodic lines that feel open and ascending, expressive and hopeful without becoming saccharine. Longer, more abstract pieces are counterbalanced by a series of shorter songs, with five vocal tracks appearing across the album. The decision to share vocal duties lends the record a unique quality and a strong sense of variation, bringing a wide expressive range out of a deliberately focused musical framework.

‘At The Emerald Pool’ represents the first chapter in an ongoing musical dialogue, an attempt to capture a moment of connection, openness and discovery, laying the foundation for what continues to unfold."

Schneidermann is a familiar face on the Copenhagen scene, working closely with Nicolas Winding Refn on the 'Valhalla Rising' score as well as the scores for each of the 'Pusher' films. And he's been a member of the Escho family for years, so it was surely only a matter of time until he collaborated with Rønnenfelt. The band rush for the '90s on 'Marble Station', layering wall-of-sound guitars with deadpan vocals, while on 'Here Comes the Dead', they sound more like Black Country heroes Slade. The band's version of 'Boy/Girl' is stronger, led by rattling hi-hats and sleazy, Suicide-style guitars and they show off their range with their surprisingly tender version of 'If Not This Time'. It's all a bit knowing, sure, but it's Copenhagen, innit.

items.body:
Oren Ambarchi and Will Guthrie reconvene for a killer, fully tooled-up fusion of organ-esque Leslie vamps, sitar-style twangs and Guthrie's Han Bennink-inspired full kit theatrics - cover art of the year included.

Ambarchi and Guthrie are both so well established by now that they can do their thing completely free from the weight of expectation, and they've been working together for so long that they seem to fully operate on instinct. They know how it goes, they're just able to flex. And this set, recorded by Rabih Beaini and Filippo Samoré at Beaini's own Morphine Raum studio-cum-venue in Berlin before it was mixed and mastered a year later by Joe Talia, might be their best to date.

On the first side, they take it as slow as they like, with Ambarchi using his Leslie setup to transform his guitar into an organ, creating sustained notes that give Guthrie the space he needs to take the lead, landing on half rhythms and skeletal sequences for a moment before shifting to the next. It works like an establishing shot, building tension and making us wait for the pay off.

On the flip, it finally comes; Ambarchi's guitar is reshaped into a machine gun of harsh feedback resonances, angrily bowed into splintered riffs and sitar-like vibrations that shatter across the sonic spectrum. Guthrie works not just to fill in the gaps, but to provide momentum, swinging boldly from hushed pattern rolls to full, explosive jazz freakouts that anticipate Ambarchi's return to the Leslie. When Ambarchi starts plucking at the strings like a man possessed, coaxing out percussive staccato melodies that almost harmonise with Guthrie's cymbal bells, it all starts to slow down into wailing, woodwind-esque bird calls.

Heavy, heady biz from the best of the best...

items.body:
The first three albums in the 'Everywhere At The End Of Time' series in one set - two and a half hours long, each album reveals new points of progression, loss and disintegration, falling further and further towards the abyss of complete memory loss and nothingness...

Embarking on the Caretaker’s final journey with the familiar vernacular of abraded shellac 78s and their ghostly waltzes to emulate the entropic effect of a mind becoming detached from everyone else’s sense of reality and coming to terms with their own, altered, and ever more elusive sense of ontology. The series aims to enlighten our understanding of dementia by breaking it down into a series of stages that provide a haunting guide to its progression, deterioration and disintegration and the way that people experience it according to a range of impending factors.

In other words, Everywhere At The End of Time probes some of the most important questions about modern music’s place in a world that’s increasingly haunted or even choked by the tightening noose of feedback loops of influence; perceptibly questioning the value of old memories as opposed to the creation of new ones, and, likewise the fidelity of those musical memories which remain, and whether we can properly recollect them from the mire of our faulty memory banks without the luxury of choice.

items.body: Austin-based composer/sound designer TJ Dumser (Six Missing) returned to roots for drift, sway—eschewing scale for intimacy in a minimal set mixing guitar loops and vintage synths with tactile timbres to create soundscapes for deep listening, reflection and filmic ambience. Subtle textures drifting in and out The recent drift, sway finds Six Missing forging what TJ Dumser describes as ‘a space where sound becomes a gentle pulse—drifting through the air like a breeze, swaying like light on water’ with pieces that purportedly ‘emerged from a meditative state, a process of dissolving into repetition, texture, and resonance,’ built ‘not […] as songs, but as movements—fluid, organic, breathing.’ Following previous releases from his ambient, meditative and cinematic project (cf. Gentle Breath, 2025), Austin-based composer/sound designer Dumser returned to roots for drift, sway—eschewing scale for intimacy in a minimal set mixing guitar loops and vintage synths with tactile timbres to create soundscapes for deep listening, reflection and filmic ambience. ‘Music for presence, for focus, for the quiet spaces within,’ he puts it, and with guitar primary he ‘let loops and delay pedals guide [him] into a trance-like flow, where melodies formed like ripples in stillness.’ A resonant realization :: Set-up/deployment (Gearhead alert!): Boss DD-20 (in 16-sec looper mode)—a vessel for layering evolving motifs; MTL.ASMLY Count to Five, Meris Mercury 7, EarthQuaker Devices Avalanche Run, Analogman King of Tone, Boomerang Looper—to shape the edges of sound into something soft yet infinite; Moog Minimoog, Korg Polysix—subtle textures drifting in and out, their warmth and imperfection breathing life into the minimal framework. The album is in two movements: Drift—six weightlessly hovering pieces reflecting the ebb-flow of thought, memory and dream; Sway—four pieces embracing stillness in motion, ‘the way we lean into presence without holding too tightly,’ the artist proffers. Overall drift, sway constitutes a resonant realization of this and the artist’s various meditative reflections. drift, sway is available on Nettwerk [Bandcamp] drift, sway by Six Missing  The post Six Missing :: drift, sway (Nettwerk) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Knowing what Foel built this record out of—a difficult mental health stretch, a fascination with landscapes that are beautiful and hostile in equal measure, a process built on chaos eventually resolving into order, Gwasgaru earns its title honestly. “Shaped randomness” Gwasgaru by Foel   Jack Smith-Keegin spent twenty years building toward this. The North Wales-based producer behind Foel started making music at sixteen, but didn’t release anything until 2025’s Ogof Melltydd single on WEPN, two decades of self-taught tool-building before he felt ready to put anything out into the world. A Welsh speaker raising two children with his wife in the mountains and coastlines of North Wales, his musical entry point traces back to hearing Boards of Canada‘s Geogaddi at fifteen, an album he describes as hitting him straight in the heart. That door opened onto Warp, Plaid, Aphex Twin, Venetian Snares, and eventually Autechre—Draft 7.30 specifically, which he says didn’t click at first but became an obsession once it did. Gwasgaru—Welsh for “scatter” or “disperse“—was built mostly in Bitwig using its modular grid, alongside a custom Node.js program with a CSound backend that Foel describes as more than vapourware but not yet fully composition-ready. His process leans heavily on repeatable randomness—generating outcomes he can hunt through and refine, rather than gravitating toward what he already knows. It’s a technical approach in service of something deeply personal: Foel made this album during what he describes as a genuinely difficult stretch with his mental health, and the record carries that weight throughout. The album’s opener is mature in its composition because i​t doesn’t set you up for anything you’d expect it to sound like. This is something deeper. The drums build into nothingness, kicks fading into the abyss of sound, layering as it continues toward the track’s end. “Rhewlif” has an interesting sound too, with its rhythm and melodic composition. At points it sounds and feels almost random, and it very well might be, nothing here sounds planned, nothing settles into a repetitive, catchy melodic pattern. That’s a deliberate choice rooted in how Foel works. Generative and randomized approaches to melody in IDM typically still operate within a defined scale or harmonic boundary, the notes are unpredictable in sequence but never unpredictable in pitch relationship, which means the result feels alive and unrepeating without ever sounding atonal or aimless. Foel‘s own description of “shaped randomness” fits exactly into that tradition. One thing already standing out in Foel‘s work is the production technique of introducing new elements midway through a long track’s build. Partway through this track, he uses very sharp filtering on the bass synth, almost like lasers cutting through the waveform—a technique close to what’s sometimes called ducking, where one sound is compressed and pushed down in response to another. In layman’s terms: imagine the bass and another element fighting for the same space, and a compressor automatically lowers the volume of one every time the other hits, so they never collide and mask each other. It’s commonly used to let a kick drum punch through a bassline in dance music, but Foel applies it more abstractly here, using it almost as a rhythmic device in its own right rather than just a mixing utility. That’s what’s happening in this track, and it genuinely gives the piece its personality as it continues, almost as if the track is disintegrating from the inside. Almost like little nothings threaded through reverb stabs and drums :: “Chwil” is another strange builder and by builder, this means Foel continues the theme of constructing anticipation across each track, whether through drums or melody, giving the listener’s ears a ride rather than a destination. Melody isn’t the focus here, which fits Foel‘s more experimental background showing through. “Dadmer” enters next and is genuinely a standout. The ducking concept reappears here, but this time the melodic note feels like it’s complementing the snare at the same moment, which creates an enjoyable experimental effect. Visually, it’s like the melody is a ping pong ball and the kick and snare are playing ping pong with it, batting it back and forth until it fades into nothing. “Ar goll” is full of dark drums and ambience that grows almost frantically in a space obsessed with reverb and compression. “Gwasgiad” functions as a part two of that idea, but cleaner in its approach, there’s a resemblance now to Autechre‘s Quaristice in its sound design sensibility, and the drum and snare programming here is genuinely excellent. The closer, “Gwasgaru,” is a dark IDM track where Foel plays the melody far back in the mix, almost like little nothings threaded through reverb stabs and drums. If there’s a theme running through this album that’s used well, it’s that ducking technique, deployed multiple times, clearly a recurring tool Foel reaches for strategically across these productions, and it’s exactly what makes them stand out as genuinely interesting to listen to. Knowing what Foel built this record out of—a difficult mental health stretch, a fascination with landscapes that are beautiful and hostile in equal measure, a process built on chaos eventually resolving into order, Gwasgaru earns its title honestly. By the closing track, that small melody really does sound like it’s floating away over the mountains, and you believe it. Art by: Ben Hendon Gwasgaru is available on Machine. items.body: Those of a certain age remember when television stations used to sign off for the night. A cheerful TV announcer would share the station identification and a pleasant goodbye, music would play (most often the national anthem) and the station would either display a static image or simply go dark. If this were the only station broadcasting, the person watching would turn off the set, and watch as the lights condensed to a dot before a final pop. Then it was time – really time – to go to bed. Few such stations remain, as the world has shifted to 24/7 access. Michael Branch (Speed of Life) recalls, “There was something magical about it. I (felt) as if I was floating outside of or removed from any notion of time.” In the digital era, it’s hard to imagine hours in which no moving images are available to view, as if nothing of any consequence is unfolding. This set of imaginary sign-off music may evoke nostalgia in older listeners and seem like sci-fi to younger listeners. The clever “Television Set” CD packaging adds to the allure. “KKZ96 (Wonder People”) begins with piano and ethereal chords, as if the mind is soaring into the imagination. As drums are folded in, one thinks of Little Nemo’s Adventures in Slumberland. The mind is left to wonder what events might be unfolding in the in-between time, unrecognized, unreported and most importantly, unbroadcast. And who are the wonder people? Are they a separate race of people active only in the invisible hours, or the images that we miss? The beatless “KCBS (Electric Lights)” dances like its namesake, without the use of percussion. The chords ebb and flow in hypnotic fashion, capturing Branch’s sense of magic. At the time, television was relatively young, and grandparents could remember when they were able to scrape enough money together for their first set: the TV itself was a wonder, a gift. Almost any broadcast seemed magical, as opposed to today, when thousands of options are available yet few possess that early allure. “KHQ6 (Visitor)” has the feel of an early black-and-white film about invaders from Mars, or from the deep, or from the Antarctic. Something otherworldly is already here, and the race is on to get other people to acknowledge their existence. It’s late at night, and Branch’s parents have gone to bed and may or may not know their son is watching; despite the fact that he has seen wonders, he cannot wake them up for fear of being punished. The next piece continues to play upon such fears, albeit gently; the chiming tones both settle and alert, an electronic pulse developing like the lights of a quietly descending spaceship, then fading slowly like a phantasm. The finale, “WTVF,” bridges the gap between the sign-off and the sign-in, hours later; guitar chords are laid atop a mysterious drone as the synthesizers vibrate, the fifteen-minute length creating a trance-like effect. Then at the very end, voices buried in static. The precocious child drifts off to sleep with one salient question on his mind: What’s on TV tomorrow? (Richard Allen)

items.body: Melbourne four-piece Karate Boogaloo wrote “Booger’s Bounce of Joy” for a dance they kept seeing at their gigs. There are no steps to it: you move every limb however you want. Callum Riley‘s organ runs the track with a growling tone, and underneath, Henry Jenkins‘s bass keeps a loose, summery groove for dancing. They recorded it live to tape with no overdubs, all four playing at once, keeping the focus entirely on a clear, hummable hook. Alongside Jenkins and Riley, percussionist and drummer Hudson Whitlock and guitarist Darvid Thor complete the quartet, the same four who play the rhythm section in Melbourne soul band The Cactus Channel. Under their own name they play instrumental funk on drums, guitar, bass and organ, a small-combo sound they take from The Meters and Booker T. & The MG’s. The four have worked Melbourne’s instrumental soul scene for over a decade: the KB’s Mixtape series came first, funk reworkings of hip-hop samples that sold out local record shops on word of mouth, and 2024’s Hold Your Horses gave them a second album of originals. They cut “Booger’s Bounce of Joy” with engineer Alex Bennett at Sound Recordings, running it through their Ampex 440 tape machine. The single comes ahead of Access All Areas, their new album for Colemine Records and College of Knowledge Records. Stream “Booger’s Bounce of Joy” HERE and pre-order Access All Areas via THIS LINK. items.body: Improvisation, especially of the largely unplanned and entirely freeform variety, can be a bit hit-and-miss, particularly when it becomes apparent that the performers aren’t singing (or playing) from the same hymn sheet. Nevertheless, when collective interactions click into place—as on this seven-track mini-album by Alexander Varty on guitar & electronics, Andres Kahre on percussion and electric cello, and violin virtuoso Jack M Campbell—the results can be truly striking and illuminating. No Room For Error came about through a serendipitous encounter between Campbell and longtime collaborators Varty and Kahre on Gabriola Island (which lies in the Strait of Georgia in British Columbia), where Varty and Kahre reside. Campbell visited the island last summer on an artist’s residency funded by the Tommy Flowers Foundation to record his first solo album, Sounding Bombe: Enigma Project. The talented violinist soon teamed up with the two musicians, with sound engineer Jordan Koop taking care of mixing and mastering, and No Room For Error was born. One becomes immediately aware of a sense of place on any island, and one of the album’s strengths is the way it conjures a particular environment, climate and atmosphere. This is never presented in a programmatic way, however, but rather sensed through the music—leaving what’s heard open to the listener’s own interpretations. For example, the uneasy, unsettling ambience evoked in the three Haar-entitled tracks relates to the Scots word for a chilly, foggy easterly wind. However, low rumbling guitars, nervously shuttling strings, glitchy sound effects, and sudden jump cuts in Haar I hint at something more sinister. Think Helmut Lachenmann trapped in a Saw movie. Haar III almost made me jump out of my skin. No room for terror would have perhaps been a more appropriate title. Meanwhile, the opening of Smir (another Scots word, this time meaning ‘fine rain’) projects a lament-like quality, eventually building to a keening Ur Schrei of powerful proportions. Not all the tracks are dark and disturbing. As its title suggests, Nightswimming is surrounded by floating, suspended lines and shimmering timbres, its subtly immersive impact aided by Varty’s use of Trope software (developed by Brian Eno and Peter Chilvers). Meanwhile, Cosmophony feels like entering inside a futuristic spaceship’s generator and experiencing its pulsing hum. No Room For Error clearly benefits from Varty and Kahre’s intuitive understanding of each other’s aims—and how best to achieve them—shaped over time through a shared Alt Jazz aesthetic and projects involving the Gabriola Microsynth Orchestra (GMO). Equally impressive is the effortless way in which Campbell fits into the ensemble’s creative dynamics, his remarkable agility tempered by an innate musicality whose instincts tell him when, or when not, to play. This special synergy is heard especially in Haar II, throughout which Campbell shines, and in the brilliant Rumbledethumps, where each member of the trio is presented in turn—tremolando-like sweeps on violin and resonant percussive patterns by Kahre, followed by gritty Robert Fripp-meets-Derek Bailey punctuations on Varty’s processed guitar. No wonder Rumbledethumps has already gained traction amongst radio stations, including BBC Radio 3’s Late Junction. It’s almost the experimental music equivalent to a Taylor Swift song. What’s more, the album’s tracks never outstay their welcome, with only Nightswimming and Smir exceeding the five-minute mark. Whether intended or not, No Room For Error hints at the title of Hank Mobley’s seminal 1963 album No Room for Squares, which featured—in addition to the trailblazing saxophonist—a veritable who’s who of jazz luminaries, such as Lee Morgan, Andrew Hill, Herbie Hancock and Philly Joe Jones. No Room For Error may not sound like Mobley’s hard bop masterpiece, but its bold, innovative improvisatory approach and boundless creativity draw on its spirit. Experimental music du jour, and endlessly creative at that. The post No Room For Error (Redshift Records) appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — This sublime group has rather rapidly taken over top spot as my favourite Spanish Prog band, a nudge beyond Rafael Pacha, only due to the impeccable quality throughout their 5-album discography, from 1997's debut "Transformation" up to today's subject matter, "Seven Hills'. Only one personnel change to announce, drummer Miguel Diaz replaces Marco Anderson, the remaining cast revolving around the incredible guitarist Raul Mannola, fluid keyboardist Denis Bilanin, Nill Oliveira on elastic bass, and Juan Carlos Aracil providing flute, a perfect detail to their flamboyant jazz-rock/fusion stylistic. While some pundits will undoubtedly mention the Mahavishnu Orchestra as an influence, I am afraid I will not take that well-trodden path, as there are some overt differences, namely the preponderant Spanish colorations as well as the soft sheen of the flute which transport the stylistics into a parallel universe perhaps by still 'miles away' from the legendary combo. One common point to note, is all five instrumentalists are exceptionally talented, and Raul Mannola is undoubtedly going to stun a few guitar fans into abject awe.The title track wastes little time in settling the listener into a comfortable mindset, a vivid reminder of just how manicured the interplay between them has endured over the years. Nearly 10 minutes of supple instrumental cohesion, the rhythm section setting the breezy pace , a musical travelogue of sorts where each instrument has a voice and a reason. The Aracil swirling around the divine, the electric guitar dancing along until it finally decides to break off the tender embrace and venture out of the comfort zone, the piano switching into rousing organ alliance that gets the juices flowing. The insanity has only just begun, as Raul rips to shreds his fretboard with raging bull fury, adding velocity to the anger, the flute coming to the rescue as if to heal the open wounds. Up to Bilanin to reveal his Brian Auger fetish with a rousing Hammond spotlight, just as intense as the axe assault, Oliveira and Diaz thrashing mightily along for the ride. What a slap in the face, I feel refreshed already ! My beloved e-piano appears to lead the band on "Blues for LC" , a tribute perhaps to either Larry Carlton or Larry Coryell (perhaps both), eventually shoring the line-up into the heady groove, a platform for Mannola, Aracil and Bilanin to trade massive slices of flurries, one wilder than the other. A slow burn finale puts out the fire, but gently. Oliveira gets to initiate the next arrangement, his eventful bass guitar lighting up the runway on "Day Five", nudging along his bandmates into a jungle feast of notes, where dense musical fruits hang from the surrounding trees, each musician picking theirs at random, savouring every bite. Bilanin goes on a piano splurge, cymbals akimbo, as if racing through an Amazonian clearing. When the bass pops, the brain gasps in delight. What an exhilarating thrill.Diaz has his turn introducing the choppy "Feel the Cool Wind ", a temperamental breeze that may switch into a gale at any moment, the flute keeping the suspense alive and well. The electric guitar first carves a swath of oblique patterns, almost Picasso-esque, until the bass and flute decide to reembrace once again, the prefect opportunity for Raul to play mind games with a wide variety of playful interventions, capturing perfectly the idiosyncrasies of an upcoming storm. The insatiable e-piano returns for another romp in the wet fields, reminding one of a Brazilian dude called Deodato. Fun. "No Return" has Raul featuring his acoustic guitar skills, a Spanish tradition to say the least, and his spot is exemplary, ably assisted by a brash rhythmic pulse, eventually revving up the engines, a slow and deliberate electric build-up that aches to explode. The only negative is that I could have enjoyed another 10 minutes of this! "Wise Raven" is definitely a finale to crow about (sorry, I had to!), a 9 minute + masterclass in bluesy jazz-rock that pretty much serves to sum up what this band has to offer. Like the petulant bird, the track is altogether brash, cocky, even pesky at times, the insistence verging on mania, with endless ebb and flow, push and pull. The Aracil flute figures to once again behave like a soothing nurse, allaying any fears that madness may prevail. Does not stop the playing to be fast and furious. The scintillating electric guitar rant gets bullied along by that throttling keyboard undertow, and Raul just takes off into the wild blue yonder. Diaz even gets to pummel his kit with notorious abandon, as if playing in concert and earning applause. Forty-one minutes of unrelenting action, emotion, spills and thrills. Que maravilla! This is a band wholly deserving of major recognition, keeping the legendary spirit of past-jazz-rock greats smiling with appreciation from above (Chick, Jaco, Joe, Wayne, Larry, Allan etc..). Muchas gracias, senores! 4.5 clear lights

items.body: Review by kev rowland — It has been quite a while since I last heard from French band Siiilk, but I was a huge fan of their 2017 album 'Endless Mysteries' and this four-track set was recorded just two years later at Les Nuits de Fourvi�re on July 21st, 2019, when they were the opening act for Nick Mason's Saucerful of Secrets. Given they were the opening act I presume this is the complete set, so we have four songs, with three from the 2012 debut and only one from the previous album. The line-up has been stable with Richard Pick (lead vocals, acoustic guitar), Catherine Pick (vocals, Indian harmonium), Gilbert Gandil (electric guitar), Jacques Roman (keyboards) and Guillaume Antoncelli (bass guitar) still there and the only change being the introduction of a new drummer, Cl�ment Vullion.In some ways this material is quite reminiscent of Hackett, but there are undoubtedly also elements of Pink Floyd, Seventies Barclay James Harvest, Camel, Caravan, and so much more. There are times when it is almost folk in its approach, at others it is pastoral while it can be somewhat driving at others. Richard's vocals do have an accent, and in many ways that is the only way to determine this is not a British act as it certainly has far more influences from across the channel than it does from France. Catherine's vocals are wonderfully clear and light, providing a contrasting dynamic to Richard while her harmonium also takes their music in a different direction and the nuanced addition of birdsong certainly feels right within the context.I missed out on their last studio album, 2022's 'Eemynor" but it was recorded by the same line-up as this, so I have high hopes and definitely need to seek it out. If you have yet to come across Siiilk then this is a great introduction and at only 5 euro is a real bargain. If you like the more thoughtful and less bombastic or experimental styles of prog then this is something you need to explore.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Formed in the early 80's by keyboard player Derk Akkermann, Saris have had different line-ups over the years combined with periods of inactivity. I enjoyed their last album, 2020's 'Beyond The Rainbow', but said there needed to be quite a few changes to be able to move ahead although I never thought they would have a total rethink of approach and alter the line-up but that is what has happened. Henrik Wager (lead & backing vocals) and Lutz G�nther (bass) are also still there, but they have now been joined by veteran proggers Jimmy Keegan (drums, percussion), Marek Arnold (saxophone) and Martin Schnella (guitars), which has changed their music in multiple ways, all for the better. More of a thematic album than a concept, it has been influenced by the state of the world, the power, the politics, the paranoia, religion and revenge, technology and temptation, corruption and contradiction. There is a need to save ourselves from others and sometime save others from ourselves, and for those of us living away from Europe, America or the Middle East, it sometimes we feel we are the only sane ones left and the world is tearing itself to pieces so I certainly understand where they are coming from.Musically this is symphonic prog combined with some prog metal, power ballads, stadium rock, melodic metal etc. Wager has a great voice, while any album which contains Schnella and Arnold will always be wonderfully arranged with many layers combining to produce something special, but in many ways this album belongs to Keegan. It is his drumming which drives through songs which may otherwise be a little bland and over-produced, creating an inventive framework for others to work around. I certainly hope this is a new band as opposed to the older members plus session musicians, as if this is what they produce the first time they are together I can't wait to see what they come up with next.The only real downside for me is a passage within "Mamucium" at the five-minute mark which is so heavily influenced by Genesis it could possibly be thought of as a "steal" from "Apocalypse in 9/8". That small point aside, this is a thoroughly enjoyable release which is easy to listen to with good hooks, wonderful vocals, and melodies. And did I mention the drumming? This is a real step up from the last album.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Having only recently come across Rob with his excellent 'Overflow' release it seemed fitting to go back a few years and investigate his 2024 debut, 'Explode My Head'. At the time of this release he was playing in both Mascot Moth and The Felix Subway Band, had co-founded Z Machine with Owen Rosser and Gareth Piper, and had been under the wing of Ian East (Gong) for four years to improve his sax playing. On this release Rob provides all guitars, saxophone, bass, vocals & sfx, but he has also brought in a few guests to make this much more of a band release as opposed to a one-man project, including the aforementioned Mr. East who contributes both flute and bass clarinet. The excellent drummer Eliseo Salverri is utilised on most tracks, and it is no surprise that Rob also used his talents on his second album.Rob is very much influenced by British progressive bands who are more experimental than many, with Cardiacs and pronk being very much the major style combined with elements of jazz fusion, Steve Hillage, Gong, Gentle Giant, VDGG, PO90 and others. Sax is sometimes the main musical lead, at others it could be the guitar, or it may even be the voice, one just never knows where this meandering musical journey is going to lead next. Often jagged, never mainstream, this is music which feels as if is from a time gone by when anything was possible with a refusal to conform to what many expect, even within the prog scene. Apparently, Rob was first influenced by guitarist Tony McPhee from The Groundhogs, a band one rarely sees mentioned today, but who released some phenomenal albums (check out 'Thank Christ for the Bomb' and 'Split', both essential), so he has a different starting point to many which undoubtedly has impacted his eccentricity.At the heart of this album is melody, but sometimes that is almost subliminal with chaos all around, yet it always makes sense. Rob is a real artist, one who goes where the muse takes him as opposed to following the herd, which is probably why he decided he needed a video to go with this so spent three frantic months building a set from scratch, making 30+ plasticene figures to inhabit it and then three long weeks of animation (for a total of about a minute and a half of footage!). The cover artwork is taken from this. There is a sense of lightness within this release, yet it refuses to compromise and the result is something which is thoroughly enjoyable indeed, and progheads looking for something a little alternative to the norm will thoroughly enjoy this.

items.body: Review by Heart of the Matter — The watchmaker steadies his delicate hand... uh, sorry, I wasn't really quoting Mr Gabriel, just thinking of that figure of an artisan with spectacles and ageing but steady hands that Steve Howe has become over so many years. And, as well as it seems perfectly true that the image and the job fit him like no other, one still has the right to ask if that is sufficient to sustain the continuation of a band's career after, again, so many years. And it may well be so, since his convoluted brilliancy shines all over this album, with lines of lush slide guitar lace, and breathtaking precision in the irregular rhythms. The best of his contribution is, of course, in the longest track, Countermovement, which reminds strongly of Double Rondo, that marvellous piece of symphonic fantasy included in his second solo effort from 1979. And that is fine with me, but don't think for a second that that is all, and the band have no proper role here. On the contrary, the rhythm section sounds muscular and precise (if not spontaneous) at the same time, the keyboards supply enough classically inspired structure as to save dignity, the orchestra do their part with an elegance excluding any excess, and the singer, finally, seems to be starting to grasp that is no duty of his to stay in the upper region of his strained vocal chords all the time, and begins to complement his efforts with Steve and the others. Not everything here is gold, but there's gold enough in the end, like those stars sprinkling in the cover.

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — 'Voice in the Light' is a 2007 concept album by progressive metal supergroup, Amaran's Plight. Featuring renowned musicians such as vocalist D.C. Cooper (Royal Hunt), guitarist Gary Wehrkamp (Shadow Gallery) and drummer Nick D'Virgilio (Spock's Beard), this ambitious release is a treat for fans of the genre, and for fans of the individuals involved. Stylistically, this sounds a lot like Shadow Gallery. Fans of the band will no doubt enjoy this, and it shows the heavy involvement of guitarist and songwriter Gary Wehrkamp. Clocking in at one hour and 19 minutes, and stretching the physical CD to its storage limits, I won't deny that I find the story a bit muddy at times. Whether it's due to the long-winded duration, or just a number of filler tracks causing me to lose interest, usually by the end of the album I'm left baffled by whatever the concept was supposed to be. Musically however, this is a very good release, with a number of particular stand-out moments. The musicianship is excellent (as you'd expect), with plenty of dazzling guitar and keyboard virtuosity, as well as fantastic vocal performances, and the album is full of both heavy and melodic tracks. Highlights include 'Truth and Tragedy', 'Turning Point', 'Betrayed By Love', 'Coming of Age', the beautiful 'Reflections Part 1', and in my opinion the highlight of the album, the energetic 'Viper'. While I doubt this is likely to be anyone's favourite album, especially as the duration can make it a bit of a slog at times, overall, 'Voice in the Light' is a very solid release, and a worthy addition to any progressive metal collection.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A meeting between guitarist Matt Stevens, drummer Stuart Marshall, and bassist Kevin Feazey, initially intended for recording Stevens' second solo �lbum, led to the formation of the band The Fierce and the Dead; they incorporated progressive elements into stoner rock and post-rock, demonstrating how well these styles blended together. For their second album, they added Steve Cleaton to the permanent lineup on second guitar, while Terry Edwards continued as a guest musician on saxophone and trumpet.Part 4 already starts with notes reminiscent of Robert Fripp, before the distortion kicks in and it follows its own path, a path of distortion, and where atonality will not be foreign. "Ark" creates guitar-driven atmospheres underpinned by drumming that at times recalls Monomyth, while "Let's Start a Cult" feels like postmodern punk rock, featuring guitar work reminiscent of Tom Verlaine from Television. Here, Terry Edwards' saxophone enters the mix, adding a welcome splash of color to the monochromatic landscape.The variety reflected in the album is striking: "Pyramid Hat" is a transcendental psychedelic funk track that bursts through the speakers; the hinted-at Eastern melody gives way to the start of "I Like It, I'm into It," where the bass takes center stage and one of the guitars seems to erupt like Fireworks, yet once those fade, the drums, bass, and a second guitar remain as a trio, continuing to dig deep into the territory where King Crimson collides with Black Sabbath."Spooky Action" sounds powerful, almost industrial, yet suddenly turns vulnerable and sensitive; one of the album's key strengths is that it retains a fresh, jam-session vibe, a sense of playfulness, and at times, its spirit reminded me of the more experimental side of The Flaming Lips."And the Bandit" is a different story: far more complex in structure and progressive, with a Yes-like feel where the ghosts of Chris Squire and Steve Howe seem to appear at times!"Entropy" evokes Adrian Belew collaborating with Toe, a major influence that is palpable throughout the album. "Part 5" revisits the tribute to Fripp, with the saxophone adding a wonderful touch, while "Chief" brings the album to a close with an air of mystery and melancholy; it is a record that shows great promise and delivers, opening doors to future sonic explorations while remaining true to the serendipitous beginnings that brought the band together when they least expected it.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Formed in 2007 and hailing from the post-hardcore scene, the Spanish band Toundra emerged as a breakout act in Spain's underground scene and performed at the 2010 Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona. The proposed sonic experience begins with "Bajamar," alternating between staggered bursts of distorted guitars and harmonic passages, with the drums providing effective accompaniment in both sections. You can feel the psychedelia; you can sense the raw, rocky texture. While the band cites Pelican, another act in the genre, as an influence, I also detect elements of Mogwai."Pleamar" unfolds in a calm, pleasant manner, albeit in black and white, and the guitar work reminded me of Mike McCready from Pearl Jam. It is on "Medusa" that the quartet truly comes together as a unit, fully utilizing the dual-guitar lineup; one can discern the two distinct paths being traced, sometimes intersecting, other times running parallel. At times, Esteban Jim�nez's guitar stands out, almost seeming to speak or gasp for breath. I also detect influences from the Badmotorfinger era of Soundgarden."�rbita" bridges psychedelia and post-rock like a desert storm, full of lightning and thunder but devoid of rain, a dry storm, where Alberto Tocados's bass plays a pivotal role, providing the counterpoints of tension and calm that link the tempestuous passages together."Jaur�a" is the closest thing to a dramatic climax on the album, a moment of heightened tension where the guitars converge to tell a sometimes somber story, a tale without words or time that, while seeming as though it had always existed, reveals itself as new with every listen.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 2026 sees the release of Muse's most relevant and diverse studio album in about two decades or so.'The Wow! Signal' is the tenth full-length studio recording from the British alternative rockdarlings and sees them bringing in producer Dan Lancaster for the first time around. Pushing thetrio to pursuit a more modern production, Lancaster definitely influenced the sound of this record,which exhibits certain similarities to other alternative bands like Bring Me the Horizon and ThreeDays Grace, with which Lancaster has also worked throughout the years. Thematically, 'The Wow!Signal' deals with space and cosmic mysteries, while some songs definitely feel like more personalstatements from Mat Bellamy. Calling this album "space rock" would then be inaccurate because itexhibits elements of alternative rock, art pop and electronic music, offering some truly proggyriffs and several unorthodox arrangements. 'The Wow! Signal' is a more of a typical maximalist Museventure that impresses with an overt-the-top energy and stunning production all throughout.In the light of this consideration, it is very interesting to hear all the different styles the bandcovers on this album. Opening their set with the unbridled and anthemic piece 'The Dark Forest', animmediate wave of nostalgic Muse pretentiousness overwhelms the listener with orchestralarrangements, anxious falsettos, and muscular guitar riffs. This is followed by 'NightshiftSuperstar', one of the most convincing singles released by the band in recent years, and anexcellent song that echoes the dance-pop aesthetic of Muse's last two albums. 'Cryogen' is anotherinteresting song that combines the art rock dynamics of earlier Muse with a futuristic electronicsound that once again reminisces the output of other contemporary alt-rock/metal acts. Later on weget 'Hexagons', which sounds like a sophisticated prog-pop number, and while it could have feltcompletely out of place on this album, the final result is actually impressive. Perhaps the mostenjoyable parts of 'The Wow! Signal' are the ones where Muse explore a darker alt-metal sound andthe tracks 'The Sickness in You & I' and 'Unravelling' are definitely fine examples. The EllieGoulding feature on 'Hush' is quite intriguing as well, as this duet actually turns out to be a veryenjoyable and unexpected entry!All in all, 'The Wow! Signal' achieves an excellent balance between modern production and nostalgicMuse maximalism. The arrangements, vocals, and overall instrumentation on this album are top-notch,and the entire thing feels like a coherent sonically intense work. On top of that, the trio deliverssome of their most compelling songs as of late. Excellent return to form from Muse!

items.body: Review by Progfan97402 — I was wondering if this would ever be accepted into Prog Archives, there's no doubt the music was worthy of inclusion and I'm glad it's now in the database. It's hard for me to think of another prog rock album that is more obscure than this. Apparently, the album did get manufactured by EMI/Electrola (but it had a generic blue label to look more like a private press) so it likely made it into standard record stores in West Germany at the time. The cover to Pacific Prison screams American private press prog album, except this isn't American at all. This does not have that professional polish, so if that's what you're wanting you won't find it here. The vocals definitely do not have that polish, either. What you get is symphonic prog with space rock overtones. Lots of Hammond organ, Elka Rhapsody, and the ARP 2600 synthesizer. It sounds like what would happen if you cross Eloy with Pulsar, and perhaps a bit of Novalis but without the polished production and a more underground feel, this is what you get. There is also some flute as well (more like Pulsar than Jethro Tull). If there is a concept behind this album it's hard telling, but all the songs segue together for one continuous listen, aside from switching from side one to side two if you own the LP. While the the shortcomings are a bit obvious, it doesn't have a great production and it definitely a bit rough around the edges, it's still a nice album worth hearing especially if you don't mind a more underground take on the German symphonic prog/space rock sound.

items.body: Take my hand, Let me show you how the night runs out Denver’s Devoratus make darkwave with a clenched jaw and a dancer’s thrust, and Vacio, their EP whose title translates from Spanish as “Empty” or “Void,” turns that tension into a lean, bruised little machine. The current lineup—Tomas on vocals, Aero on synths, Renee on bass, and Cisco adding live guitar—works from familiar gothic materials, yet the record has a focused personality: dry humour at the edge of despair, Spanish-language ache beside English plainspokenness, and club velocity pressed against private collapse. The production favors cold angles and thick low end. Synth parts hang in the air like metal under moonlight, while Renee’s bass gives each track a stalking physicality. Aero’s keys cut through with glassy discipline, sometimes framing the beat, sometimes needling it, while the guitar’s presence traces the shadows into a sharper human shape. Tomas sings as if addressing someone across a locked room, his voice grave, close, and melancholic, carrying the EP’s themes of isolation, desire, mortality, and change without turning them into costume drama or diary theater. Abismo oscuro comes out of the gate with an icy guitar line, cold synths settling over it like a layer of winter frost. The drumming pushes forward with almost punk impatience, while the shadowy vocal line rides the rush with a sense of momentum, doom, and romantic wreckage that recalls Lowlife at their darkest. Lyrically, the song stares straight into death’s mirror: sin is abandoned, the cross is taken up, the end is declared present, and the body is returned to dust. Its devotional language and blunt mortality give the track a ritual severity, less like melodrama than an alarm bell ringing in a freezing room. The song moves fast without losing its shape, giving its gloom a sharp edge rather than letting it dissolve into decorative fog. It lands with urgency, not clutter. Dance is the release’s most direct invitation to the floor, though its pleasure has a sickly grin. Echoed vocals stretch across atmospheric synths, and the rhythm keeps the body busy while the mind wanders toward less friendly rooms. The lyrics turn the dance floor into both seduction and survival: the Spanish lines suggest instruction, surrender, and a refusal to look back, while the English refrain reaches outward like a hand in the dark. It is not escapism exactly, but movement as a last practical response to ruin. Dance music can carry dread without collapsing into theatre; Devoratus understand that the best grooves can feel useful, almost medicinal, as if motion itself were the only thing keeping the void from closing in. For You keeps the tempo high but aims closer to the chest. It plays as a fast ballad for someone already gone or maybe still too near, with echo, ache, and forward drive braided into a clean blow. The narrator wakes disoriented, caught in the repetition of not knowing where they are, unable to stop living inside the self. When the song turns toward Spanish, that private confusion becomes a plea for an ending and a way out, not simply for escape, but for another person. That shift gives the track its emotional weight. It is wounded without becoming helpless, romantic without becoming soft. The restraint gives the record leverage: Devoratus leave enough space around the parts, so every bass note, drum hit, guitar slash, and vocal bend lands with intention. Vacio is compact, stylish, and severe, yet it breathes. Its emptiness is not blankness, but pressure: the absence one dances through, prays against, wakes inside, and tries to outrun. Fans of Forever Grey, Lebanon Hanover, She Past Away, and other cold-hearted romantics will recognize the alleyways it traverses, but Devoratus walk them with their own private map. This is gothic dance music with bite, brains, and bleak charge for rooms already leaning toward the dark. items.body: Brooklyn synth duo Observation Room have spent the last few years finding the heart beating inside the machine. On Superstructure, their debut full-length for à La Carte Records, Marina F and Chloe Olson expand the hypnotic precision of their self-titled EP into something stranger, warmer, and more textural: synth-pop with its circuitry exposed and the windows cracked open. The record keeps the duo’s precise electronic chill intact, but fattens it with breath, doubt, humour, and a bright ache that makes you suspect the machines have been listening while you talk in your sleep. Observation Room have made synth-pop with blood pressure: bright surfaces, nervous systems, and a brain full of alarms. Superstructure is smart, strange, physical, and wide awake, grinning hard under the emergency lights. The first single, Running Lights, works as both invitation and warning flare. It locks into a headlight-after-headlight momentum, steady enough for the dance floor but too keyed-up to dissolve into lifestyle wallpaper. The pulse is sleek, but not passive; every repetition seems to tighten the room by a few degrees. When the chorus finally opens, it feels earned, like a locked stairwell suddenly giving onto sky. Running Lights draws its charge from the duo’s devotion to process, pressure, and disciplined play. The reference points are clear enough: Depeche Mode’s severe romance, Book of Love’s gloss, OMD’s machine-pop manners, plus older electronic cousins from krautrock, Tangerine Dream, and early Human League. But Observation Room are not simply arranging their influences into a tasteful mood board. They keep their hands on the method. They build small systems, repeat them, compress them, and wait for strange colours to leak out. Listen to Running Lights below. Superstructure arrives September 11. Pre-order here. Superstructure by Observation Room The album’s title, Superstructure, carries a clean, glassy double charge. On one side is architecture: the frame, the scaffold, the built environment. On the other is ideology: the unseen system that tells the body where to move, what to fear, and how to behave. Across the LP, private panic keeps finding its public wiring. Surveillance begins as a twitch behind the eyes, then expands into policy, screens, money, cops, bosses, feeds, and all the little invisible rails that teach people where to stand. Marina F and Olson, sharpened by political organizing and dread, treat anxiety not as a personal defect but as something manufactured, maintained, and, in certain flashes, danced through. The production, handled and mixed by Marina F in Brooklyn, gives the record depth, pressure, and enough space for its uglier textures to breathe. Mechanical bloops, field recordings, dissonant corners, and thick low-end touches from 90s house press against vocal harmonies shaped by rooms full of bodies. The result is both intimate and civic, club-lit and fluorescent, as if the songs were built for headphones, basement speakers, and the nervous walk home afterward. Sharon Aiza Engel’s mastering gives the album firm edges without draining its glow. items.body: SEKTION, the project of German electronic musicians AtomTM (Uwe Schmidt) and Siegmar Fricke, release “Druck“, their first full-length album, on Geometrik Records, out 17 July 2026 as a limited black vinyl LP of 250 copies. The record moves through industrial and experimental electronic territory across thirteen tracks and marks the first official SEKTION collaboration between the two, a connection the pair trace back to 1992. SEKTION detail ‘Druck’ and its structure “Druck” is built from four compositional frameworks that Schmidt and Fricke title Vokostasis, Digitraktion, Leerzeichen and Unwucht. The thirteen tracks follow those groups in sequence: four “Vokostasis” pieces and four “Digitraktion” pieces on the first side, then two “Leerzeichen” edits and three “Unwucht” edits on the second. The duo shape metallic textures, granular rhythms and slow structural shifts, with frequency-altered voice fragments and layers of tape noise running through the record. Geometrik Records has posted four excerpts from the album on SoundCloud. The album is the first SEKTION full-length. It follows “Kopplung”, a two-track SEKTION release issued in May 2025. Geometrik Records is the Madrid label associated with Spanish industrial group Esplendor Geométrico. About SEKTION SEKTION pairs Uwe Schmidt and Siegmar Fricke, two German artists whose work reaches back to the late 1980s and early 1990s. Schmidt, born on 27 August 1968 in Frankfurt am Main, has recorded prolifically since 1988 under names that include Atom TM, Atom Heart, Lassigue Bendthaus and Señor Coconut. He co-founded the label Rather Interesting with Pete Namlook and has released through Raster-Noton, Fax and Mille Plateaux, among others. His work ranges across techno, ambient, industrial and electrolatino, and his Señor Coconut album “El Baile Alemán” (2000) reworked Kraftwerk as Latin dance music. As a producer and remixer he has worked with Ryuichi Sakamoto, Haruomi Hosono of Yellow Magic Orchestra, Depeche Mode, Merzbow and Towa Tei, and he has reconstructed and remixed material by Esplendor Geométrico. In July 2024, Uwe H. Schmidt headlined the Russian Outline festival, which returned after its last edition in 2016, and this amid the ongoing conflict with Ukraine. It didn’t take long before critics, such as Ukrainian activist Maya Baklanova, rightfully said that Western artists performing in Russia were normalizing the war and supporting the Russian regime by their participation. Siegmar Fricke began experimenting with shortwave radio and acoustic noise around 1981, in the space between musique concrète and post-industrial sound, and became an active figure in the international cassette-culture network. He ran his own label, Bestattungsinstitut, and issued numerous tapes between 1985 and 1993 spanning experimental music, EBM and ambient. Since the 2000s he has worked mainly as Pharmakustik, and his collaborations include work with Conrad Schnitzler and Maurizio Bianchi. “Druck” brings the two together as SEKTION for their first album, extending a working relationship the pair date to 1992.

items.body: Devoratus, a darkwave band from Denver, Colorado, released the “Vacio” EP on 4 July 2026. The three-track record is sung in Spanish and English and is available to stream on Spotify. The title translates from Spanish as “empty” or “void.” The EP’s three tracks are “Abismo oscuro,” “Dance” and “For You.” The songs move between Spanish titles and lyrics and English refrains, the bilingual approach the band has used since its first releases in 2023. Across the three tracks the band addresses isolation, desire, mortality and change. Inside the Devoratus ‘Vacio’ EP Devoratus records as a trio of Tomas on vocals, Aero on synths and Renee on bass, with Cisco adding live guitar. On “Vacio” the arrangements pair cold synth lines and heavy low end with guitar and forward-driving drums. The band released the EP without a label credit, as a digital release; no physical edition has been announced. Musically the band can be compared to darkwave acts including Lebanon Hanover and She Past Away. About Devoratus Devoratus is a darkwave and post-punk band from Denver, Colorado. The band describes itself as a “Post Punk Darkwave Latino Band” and sings in both Spanish and English. Its recording lineup is Tomas on vocals, Aero on synths and Renee on bass, with Cisco on live guitar. The band began releasing music in 2023, starting with the single and video “Distancia” and the “Amissus” EP the same year. In February 2024 Devoratus issued the single “Flotando,” followed later in 2024 by the three-track “Vida Irreal” EP, made up of “Cold Night,” “Mal” and “Vampira.” Those earlier releases remain on the band’s Bandcamp page. With the “Vacio” EP on 4 July 2026, Devoratus continues the Spanish-and-English darkwave it has released since 2023.

The Barcelona-based band confirmed the schedule through their official channels, with the UK leg running from 3 to 6 September and the Spanish dates set for late September and Halloween. The UK shows place Larva on Massive Ego’s first headline UK tour, the “Symphony Of Flies Tour”, which the British darkwave act built around their 2026 album for Out Of Line Music. Most of the catalogue has appeared through the Hungarian label Advoxya Records, and the project has worked the European dark-electro circuit for more than two decades, performing as a duo. items.body: Dead Voices on Air, the project of Mark Spybey, will release a new album, “Mothcomma”, worldwide through Re:Mission Entertainment on 17 July 2026. The 12-track album comes out on CD and in digital form, with pre-orders open at Bandcamp and the project’s Big Cartel store. Dead Voices on Air recorded “Mothcomma” in the aftermath of the project’s 2025 US tour, with sessions split between the Tees Valley in North East England and Lafayette, Colorado. The album was made on both sides of the Atlantic, and mixes the project’s experimental, industrial and dark ambient elements, moving between song structures, ambient passages, hand-built rhythms and treated vocals. Named tracks include “Pas de Chasse”, the title track “Mothcomma” and “For the Rush of Black Tar”. Mothcomma by Dead Voices on Air Recording and credits behind Dead Voices on Air ‘Mothcomma’ The album credits Nathan Jamiel, Mark Spybey and Stephen Weatherall, with additional contributions from Robert Galbraith and Elizabeth Virosa of Snowbeasts and from Lori Cole. Robert Galbraith mastered the record. Nathan Jamiel, of the Denver band The Drood, and Stephen Weatherall have contributed to the project’s last two albums and played Spybey’s autumn 2025 US concerts. Pre-orders run through Bandcamp and the Big Cartel store, where the “Mothcomma” CD is listed alongside a new run of t-shirts. Stock is limited: some items ship from the United States and others directly from Spybey in the UK, and the first 40 orders include a Dead Voices on Air logo sticker. About Dead Voices on Air Dead Voices on Air formed in Vancouver in 1992, when Mark Spybey, who had played in Newcastle’s Zoviet France in the late 1980s, began the project with Scott Harker and Clancy Dennehey. It became the ongoing vehicle for Spybey’s experimental, industrial and dark ambient work. Spybey was also an original member of Download, the offshoot featuring Skinny Puppy’s cEvin Key, and recorded under the name Propeller. Across more than three decades, Spybey has collaborated widely, working with Graham Lewis of Wire, Faust, Michael Rother of Neu!, Dieter Moebius of Cluster, Jarboe of Swans, Jochen Arbeit of Einstürzende Neubauten, Lee Scratch Perry, Pigface and Snowbeasts. He has released through labels including Cold Spring, Soleilmoon, Kranky, Nettwerk, Emergency Hearts and Re:Mission Entertainment, and works with Zoviet France co-founder Robin Storey as Reformed Faction. In 2022 Emergency Hearts published Spybey’s musical memoir “Explicit in Purpose”. Side-Line has followed the project in recent years, from the 2022 re-release of its debut as “Abrader Redux” to the 2023 collaborative album “Pennine” with Xqui, and spoke with Spybey for a 2021 ‘Click Interview’. In spring 2023 Spybey formed DADU with friends from his home town; Nathan Jamiel and Stephen Weatherall, who feature on “Mothcomma”, came out of that circle and toured the US with him in 2025. “Mothcomma” is the project’s newest release for Re:Mission Entertainment.

The album balances stripped-back minimalism with heavier machine rhythms, feedback and white noise, set against slower melodic passages.
